We next challenged P7 neonates and 4-week-old mice using either an acute high-dose model to mimic fulminant infection, analysed at 4 h, or a single low-dose challenge with prolonged follow-up to approximate residual toxin activity after antibiotic clearance, analysed at days 5–7. Across both age groups and dosing strategies, Delta toxin induced a severe NEC-like multiorgan pathology. Intestines showed mucosal disruption, villus destruction, epithelial detachment and oedema (Fig. 2c,d and Extended Data Fig. 2c,d). Concurrently, the brain exhibited haemorrhage, ependymal disorganization, periventricular oedema, ventricular dilation (Fig. 2e,f and Extended Data Fig. 2e,f), neuronal shrinkage and degeneration, and inflammatory cell infiltration (Fig. 2g,h and Extended Data Fig. 2g–i). We also observed intravascular coagulation within the cerebral microvasculature in the hippocampal region (Extended Data Fig. 2j,k). In 4-week-old mice, brain MRI further confirmed that Delta toxin caused brain injury and ventricle dilation (Fig. 2i,j), mirroring the neuropathology observed in patients with NEC. In vivo photoacoustic imaging of brains showed a significant reduction in cerebral blood flow, vascular density and branching index, indicating Delta-toxin-associated hypoxic–ischaemic injury and cognitive impairment (Fig. 2k,l).

Beyond the brain, Delta toxin induced widespread multiorgan pathology, with particularly severe injury observed in the kidney and lung. These tissues exhibited distinct signs of coagulopathy, haemorrhage and inflammatory cell infiltration, notably affecting the renal medulla, glomeruli and pulmonary parenchyma in both age groups (Extended Data Fig. 2l–o). Moreover, toxin-treated mice showed dilated ear vessels and increased Evans blue extravasation in the peritoneal lavage fluid, indicating vascular damage25 (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). Delta toxin further induced systemic coagulation abnormalities, including elevated red blood cell counts, reduced platelets and altered coagulation parameters, including prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time,  and reduced fibrinogen (Extended Data Fig. 3c–h). These findings recapitulate the severe disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) observed in Delta-toxin-positive patients with NEC (Fig. 1e). Inflammasome activation is known to drive coagulation through macrophage-mediated release of tissue factor26. Consistently, Delta toxin promoted tissue factor release from macrophages and Caco2 intestinal epithelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 3i), suggesting that both cell types contribute to toxin-induced coagulopathy.

To define the specific contribution of Delta toxin to neurological injury, we evaluated the effects of Beta toxin, which has been implicated in type C C. perfringens enteritis27. Beta toxin exhibited selective cytotoxicity for endothelial HUVECs but notably spared HT-29 intestinal epithelial cells and organoids (Extended Data Fig. 4a–c), aligning with a previous report that Beta toxin preferentially targets CD31+ vascular endothelial cells28. In vivo, it induced rapid, dose-dependent mortality (Extended Data Fig. 4d), but did not induce brain pathology at any dose tested (Extended Data Fig. 4e). These data demonstrate the specific pathogenic role of Delta toxin as a driver of NEC-like multiorgan pathology.

We next examined whether Delta-toxin-induced brain injury is associated with blood–brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction and neuroinflammation. In 4-week-old mice, Evans blue extravasation revealed dose-dependent BBB leakage after Delta toxin challenge, with lipopolysaccharide (LPS)29 as a positive control (Fig. 2m–o). Acute high-dose Delta toxin (100 μg, 8 h) caused more-severe BBB disruption than either prolonged low-dose Delta toxin (20 μg, analysed at day 7) or acute LPS (1 mg, 8 h), indicating that Delta toxin rapidly disrupts BBB integrity. ZO-1 immunofluorescence in the hippocampus confirmed structural damage with localized disorganization and reduced signal intensity (Fig. 2p,q).

BBB disruption is often accompanied by neuroinflammation30,31 and intestinal CD4+ T cells migrate across the BBB into the brain, where they accumulate with microglia to trigger neuroinflammation32,33. We next characterized brain immune cell populations after exposure to Delta toxin. In both age groups, acute high-dose Delta toxin triggered an increase in total CD45+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 5a). This increase was largely attributable to a marked expansion of the microglial population, predominantly reflecting microglial expansion (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c), confirmed by increased IBA1+ immunostaining (Extended Data Fig. 5d–g). Three-dimensional analysis revealed a shift of microglia from ramified to amoeboid morphology, characterized by shorter branch lengths and attenuated processes (Extended Data Fig. 5d–g). GFAP+ astrocytes also increased, with increased branching and cell volume (Extended Data Fig. 5h–k), indicating pro-inflammatory activation34. CD4+ and CD8+ T cells remained at similar levels at this timepoint (Extended Data Fig. 5l). In neonates after low-dose prolonged challenge, microglial expansion and activation (Extended Data Fig. 5m–r) were accompanied by increased CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Extended Data Fig. 5s,t), consistent with T cell recruitment 4 days after NEC induction32.

As patients with NEC exhibit a pronounced systemic and central nervous system inflammatory response1, we analysed cytokine profiles in the serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of patients with NEC positive for C. perfringens Delta toxin. The results revealed abnormally high cytokine levels, including IL-6, IL-10, TNF and IL-1β (Fig. 3a,b). To examine whether Delta toxin contributes to this inflammatory activation, we administered Delta toxin to 4-week-old mice through i.p. injection and observed a significant increase in IL-1β levels in both the serum and peritoneal fluid (Fig. 3c), along with a dose-dependent upregulation of Il1b, Il18, Tnf and Nlrp3 mRNA levels in peritoneal lavage cells (Fig. 3d). IL-1β and IL-18 are major effector cytokines released after NLRP3 inflammasome activation35, and activated macrophages represent the principal cellular source of mature IL-1β36. The specific NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950 suppressed Delta-toxin-induced Il1b and Il18 in peritoneal macrophages (Fig. 3e), improved survival rates (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 6a) and mitigated Delta-toxin-induced BBB disruption, as evidenced by reduced Evans blue extravasation (Fig. 3g,h). These findings suggest that Delta toxin activates the NLRP3 inflammasome to drive local and systemic inflammation as well as BBB damage.

We next examined whether macrophages, well-established cells capable of NLRP3 inflammasome activation, are preferentially targeted by Delta toxin. In both neonates and 4-week-old mice, high-dose Delta toxin caused rapid, near-complete depletion of peritoneal macrophages within 1 h, and low-dose exposure resulted in reduced peritoneal macrophage numbers persisting for 5–7 days (Fig. 3i,j and Extended Data Fig. 6b–d). By contrast, neutrophils decreased at 1 h, accumulated by 4 h and persisted to days 5–7, suggesting a subsequent neutrophil-dominated inflammatory response (Fig. 3i,j and Extended Data Fig. 6b–d). In the neonatal intestine, Delta toxin selectively depleted macrophages, without significantly altering T cells, B cells, neutrophils or dendritic cells (Fig. 3k,l and Extended Data Fig. 6e,f). Consistently, neonatal mice infected with the NCTC3181 (Delta toxin+) strain showed both a reduced percentage and a reduced absolute number of intestinal macrophages at 4 days after infection, whereas infection with the CVCC1160 strain (Delta toxin−) resulted in no detectable change (Fig. 3m). To assess the inflammatory potency relative to other PFTs, we exposed primary peritoneal macrophages to Staphylococcus aureus α-haemolysin (α-Hla), C. perfringens Delta toxin, Beta toxin, Pfo or LPS. Macrophages were resistant to α-Hla, Beta toxin and Pfo, but exceptionally sensitive to Delta toxin (Fig. 3n). Delta toxin potently induced inflammatory cytokine mRNA at 1–5 ng ml−1, whereas Pfo and α-Hla required around 5,000 ng ml−1 and 50,000 ng ml−1, respectively; Beta toxin had a minimal effect even at high concentrations. Notably, Delta toxin was effective at approximately 100-fold lower concentrations than LPS (Fig. 3o). Consistently, IL-1β was detected in primary peritoneal macrophage culture supernatants after 10 ng ml−1 Delta toxin treatment (Fig. 3p).

To define the mechanism, we examined key inflammatory cell-death pathways in immortalized bone-marrow-derived macrophages (iBMDMs). Delta toxin induced a time-dependent increase in pyroptosis signatures, including accumulation of pro-caspase-1, cleaved caspase-1 and gasdermin D (Fig. 3q). By contrast, canonical apoptosis markers, BAX induction and caspase-3 cleavage37 were not detectably altered under the same conditions (Fig. 3r), supporting pyroptosis as the dominant cell-death program induced by Delta toxin in iBMDMs.

We next tested whether K+ efflux38, a conserved trigger for NLRP3 inflammasome activation after membrane permeabilization, mediates Delta-toxin-induced inflammation. Extracellular KCl, used to prevent intracellular K+ depletion, abrogated Delta-toxin-induced NLRP3 upregulation and caspase-1 cleavage (Extended Data Fig. 6g), identifying K+ efflux as a major upstream signal. Moreover, Delta toxin rapidly induced ERK phosphorylation (Fig. 3s), consistent with pore-forming toxin-induced calcium influx, which subsequently activates MAPK–ERK signalling39. In vivo, bone marrow cells from Delta-toxin-treated mice showed increased GSDMD cleavage (Fig. 3t), confirming pyroptotic signalling. Collectively, these findings reveal that Delta toxin drives potent inflammation through the NLRP3–Caspase-1–GSDMD pathway and activates MAPK–ERK signalling.

We next examined whether Delta toxin engages a specific host receptor to mediate cell binding and cytotoxicity. We first evaluated the sensitivity of various cell lines. HeLa and HT29 cells were found to be highly susceptible, indicating that they abundantly express receptor (Extended Data Fig. 7a). We therefore performed a genome-wide CRISPR–Cas9 screen in HeLa cells using the GeCKO v2 library40 against Delta toxin (0.01 μg ml−1) (Fig. 4a). Next-generation sequencing of surviving cells revealed Cd9 as the top hit (Fig. 4b). CD9 expression was confirmed across relevant cell lines, and higher CD9 expression was associated with increased sensitivity to Delta toxin (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 7a). Although Delta toxin has been reported to bind to GM221, genetic disruption (UGCG knockout (KO)) or pharmacological inhibition (EtDO-P4 treatment) of GlcCer-derived glycosphingolipids (including most gangliosides such as GM2) did not change cellular sensitivity (Extended Data Fig. 7b,c). By contrast, CD9-KO rendered HeLa cells resistant to Delta toxin with toxicity reduced by around 40,000-fold (Fig. 4d). Moreover, CD9-overexpressing (CD9-GFP-oe) A549 cells showed markedly increased sensitivity (Fig. 4e). KO of other candidate genes (LRP6 and CLEC12B) did not alter toxin sensitivity (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 7d). GST-tagged Delta toxin can bind to wild-type (WT) HeLa cells and CD9-GFP-oe A549 cells, but not to CD9-KO cells and A549 cells (Fig. 4f–h). Biolayer interferometry (BLI) assays confirmed specific binding between GST–CD9 and Delta toxin, but not Beta toxin (Fig. 4i). The measured interaction (KD) fell in the micromolar-range binding affinity, indicative of specific, low-affinity binding (Extended Data Fig. 7e,f). It is possible that a proper membrane environment is required for the high-affinity binding of Delta toxin on cell surfaces. Together, these data identify CD9 as a receptor for Delta toxin.

Human CD9 is a member of the tetraspanin family, containing four transmembrane domains, short cytoplasmic N and C protein termini, a short extracellular domain (EC1) and a long EC241 (Fig. 4j). To map the functional binding determinant, we first performed CD9 mutagenesis analyses. Disrupting EC1 by inserting a 3×Flag tag at three independent positions did not impair GST–Delta toxin binding when EC1 mutants were re-expressed in CD9-KO cells (Extended Data Fig. 8a), indicating that EC1 is dispensable for toxin targeting.

We next conducted domain-swap experiments with human CD82, which is structurally similarity to CD942 (Fig. 4j). Only CD9 mutants containing the EC2 domain retained the ability to bind to Delta toxin, whereas mutants with the EC2 domain replaced by that of CD82 did not interact with the Delta toxin (Fig. 4k and Extended Data Fig. 8b). To further confirm the functional requirement of the EC2 domain, we used a function-blocking antibody specifically targeting the CD9 EC2 domain. Immunostaining demonstrated exclusive binding to cells overexpressing WT CD9, but not to CD9 chimeras in which the EC2 domain was substituted with that of CD82 (Fig. 4l). This antibody protected HeLa cells from Delta-toxin-induced cytotoxicity (Fig. 4m).

We next evaluated species selectivity of the Delta toxin–CD9 interaction. CD9-KO cells reconstituted with CD9 homologues from multiple vertebrate species, including Mus musculus, Bos taurus, Sus scrofa, Danio rerio and Gallus domesticus, supported toxin binding, whereas reconstitution with Drosophila or Caenorhabditis elegans homologues did not (Extended Data Fig. 8c), suggesting that toxin binding depends on a conserved region across mammals. Sequence alignment revealed that EC2 is broadly conserved among toxin-binding species but diverges in Drosophila and C. elegans (Extended Data Fig. 8d). These results collectively indicate that CD9 is a specific cell surface receptor for Delta toxin, with the EC2 domain mediating binding and cytotoxicity. Single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis of intestinal cells43 showed that CD9 is highly expressed in monocytes and intestinal epithelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 8e). Flow cytometry analysis confirmed higher CD9 expression in macrophages than in other major intestinal immune cell populations (Extended Data Fig. 8f). These results are consistent with the strong cytotoxicity of Delta toxin toward macrophages and HT29 cells that we observed. CD9 expression patterns therefore dictate the cellular tropism of the Delta toxin.

To determine whether CD9 is functionally required in vivo, we generated Cd9f/f mice and crossed them with EllaiCre (systemic Cd9-KO), Lyz2cre (myeloid) or Vil1iCre (intestinal epithelial) mice for lineage-specific deletion. Western blotting confirmed loss of CD9 protein in BMDMs from Cd9-KO mice (Extended Data Fig. 9a). After lethal Delta toxin challenge, all WT mice died within 20 h, whereas Cd9-KO mice were completely protected, maintained body weight and activity, and showed reduced disease severity (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Fig. 9b). Myeloid-specific Cd9 deletion also conferred strong protection, while intestinal epithelial-specific deletion delayed mortality, indicating partial protection (Fig. 5a).

Consistent with improved survival, Cd9-KO mice showed reduced intestinal, lung and kidney pathology (Fig. 5b,c), and their intestines remained morphologically normal after toxin challenge (Fig. 5d). Intestinal organoids derived from Cd9-KO mice demonstrated resistance to the Delta-toxin-induced cytotoxicity (Extended Data Fig. 9c). BBB integrity and lung haemorrhage were preserved in Cd9-KO mice (Cd9-KO, Cd9f/fLyz2cre and Cd9f/fVil1iCre mice) (Fig. 5e,f). Ear engorgement and DIC-like phenotypes, including thrombocytopaenia and hypofibrinogenaemia, were markedly attenuated in Cd9-KO mice (Extended Data Fig. 9d,e). Notably, Delta-toxin-induced macrophage depletion and subsequent neutrophilic accumulation were rescued in Cd9-KO and Cd9f/fLyz2cre mice but not in Cd9f/fVil1iCre mice (Fig. 5g,h and Extended Data Fig. 9f), correlating with reduced serum IL-1β levels and Il1b mRNA expression in BMDMs (Fig. 5i and Extended Data Fig. 9g), suggesting an overall dampening of the inflammatory response. Cd9f/fVil1iCre mice also displayed partially reduced IL-1β levels, consistent with its partial survival protection after challenge with Delta toxin (Fig. 5a).

We next validated the requirement for CD9 during Delta toxin+ C. perfringens infection in neonatal mice. The survival outcomes and multiorgan damage phenotypes of mice were consistent with those observed after Delta toxin challenge (Extended Data Fig. 9h–j). These results demonstrate that CD9 is required for Delta toxin toxicity in vivo by facilitating macrophage targeting, activating inflammatory cascades and driving lethal multiorgan injury.

As Delta toxin triggers systemic pathology, we examined whether toxin neutralization could be used as a therapeutic strategy. We generated a neutralizing monoclonal antibody against Delta toxin by immunizing mice with a non-toxic Delta toxin mutant (V17E/T18E), validated by a cell viability assay (Extended Data Fig. 10a). The selected monoclonal antibody bound to Delta toxin with high affinity (Extended Data Fig. 10b), protected RAW264.7 cells from toxin-induced cytotoxicity (Extended Data Fig. 10c,d) and suppressed Delta-toxin-induced Il1b and Ccl2 expression (Extended Data Fig. 10e).

We next investigated the therapeutic efficacy of the monoclonal antibody in C. perfringens-induced NEC. Pups received anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody or IgG before and during gavage with Delta toxin+ C. perfringens from P7 to P11 (Fig. 5j). Anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody treatment improved survival after infection with the clinical-03 and NCTC3181 strains (Fig. 5k) preserved intestinal crypt-villus architecture with reduced inflammatory infiltration (Fig. 5l,m and Extended Data Fig. 10f), attenuated lateral ventricle and ependymal disruption in the brain (Fig. 5n,o and Extended Data Fig. 10g) and reduced lung injury, including septal thickening and haemorrhage (Extended Data Fig. 10h,i). These findings suggest that Delta toxin is a virulence factor driving C. perfringens-induced NEC, and therapeutic neutralization of this toxin offers a promising strategy for preventing lethal pathology.

NEC was considered to be a multifactorial syndrome driven by prematurity and environmental stress. Our findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a disorder mediated by a specific bacterial toxin. By identifying C. perfringens Delta toxin as a key virulence factor, we define a molecular mechanism that is sufficient to drive intestinal necrosis and remote cerebral injury. Notably, this toxin-based mouse model reproduces major clinical symptoms without exogenous stressors, such as hypoxia or hypothermia, that are typically required in current commonly used models. This result suggests that rather than acting solely as an opportunistic colonizer of a compromised gut, C. perfringens can function as a primary initiator of barrier failure and a key driver for the systemic progression of NEC. This mechanism is consistent with the enrichment of Delta-toxin-positive strains in fatal clinical cases, suggesting a direct link between bacterial virulence and the systemic progression of fulminant NEC. The prevalence of Delta-toxin-positive infection is probably underestimated. Antibiotic treatment, common in NEC, can rapidly reduce faecal bacterial loads, thereby limiting stool culture-based detection. Serologic detection of Delta-toxin-specific antibodies provides a complementary strategy to unmask previous infection with Delta-toxin-producing C. perfringens in patients with NEC.

NEC-associated brain injury is linked to systemic and central nervous system inflammation. CD4+ T cells were detectable in the developing brain in experimental NEC and human specimens, contributing to neuroinflammation and white-matter injury. This adaptive immune component is typically evaluated at later stages of experimental NEC (around 4 days after NEC induction32). Our findings add a toxin-driven dimension by identifying a microbial toxin that elicits rapid innate immune activation with early brain injury. A notable feature of Delta toxin exposure is the speed and magnitude of the response: macrophages were nearly depleted within around 1 h after challenge, followed by systemic inflammation, BBB disruption and rapid microglial activation. At examined timepoints, brain immune profiling revealed increased CD45+ immune cells dominated by microglial changes, whereas T cell proportions were not detectably altered on the basis of flow cytometry. At day 5 in the low-dose neonates, both CD4+ and CD8+ T cell numbers were increased, aligning with previous NEC models. These data suggest that Delta-toxin-associated brain injury is initially dominated by innate immune mechanisms, and likely later shapes or amplifies adaptive immune contributions. Notably, Delta toxin was undetectable within the brain during bacterial infection and toxin challenge, indicating that brain injury is probably driven by systemic inflammation rather than direct brain toxin accumulation. Consistent with this, the NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950 blocked peripheral IL-1β maturation, preserved BBB tight-junction integrity and prevented remote brain pathology without directly altering the toxin itself.

If innate activation represents the initial wave of injury, the key question is how inflammation is amplified so rapidly. PFTs, including Pfo, have been reported to activate NLRP344. Across the toxins tested, Delta toxin induced the strongest cytokine response, notably at sublytic doses at which other PFTs elicited minimal induction. Consistent with this severity, Delta toxin produced marked BBB disruption in vivo—exceeding that observed with LPS, a benchmark for inflammation-associated BBB injury29. This inflammatory gain is mechanistically explained by the toxin’s preferential targeting of macrophages, where it engages inflammasome signalling to trigger GSDMD-dependent pyroptosis. This establishes macrophages as highly sensitive sensors that convert toxin exposure into a systemic cytokine storm. Consistent with this, a study recently reported that the PFT aerolysin preferentially depletes gut-resident macrophages, promoting intestinal inflammation and epithelial barrier vulnerability45.

We identified the tetraspanin CD9 as a host protein receptor required for Delta toxin. This aligns with a growing paradigm in which host membrane proteins act as key receptors for PFTs and define their tropism, for example, S. aureus α-Hla with ADAM1046, C. perfringens Beta-toxin with CD3128, and Enterococcus Epx2 with MHC class I47. Previous studies showed that Delta toxin binds to GM2 gangliosides in cell-free liposome systems21. However, in mammalian cell assays, genetic disruption of glycosphingolipid synthesis by UGCG KO or pharmacological inhibition with EtDO-P4 did not detectably alter Delta toxin sensitivity. These results suggest that GlcCer-derived glycosphingolipids are not essential for Delta toxin cytotoxicity on the plasma membrane. Other membrane components such as cholesterol-enriched domains may contribute to pore assembly and membrane insertion48. Genetic ablation of Cd9 markedly attenuated Delta-toxin-associated intestinal injury, BBB leakage and neuroinflammation, placing the Delta toxin–CD9 axis as a potential therapeutic target. CD9 also raises an interesting link to extracellular vesicle biology49. CD9 is a common tetraspanin marker enriched on extracellular vesicles, implicated as carriers of inflammatory signals in systemic infection and organ injury. Given that extracellular vesicles act as protective decoys that trap PFTs50, and that Delta toxin specifically targets extracellular-vesicle-associated CD9, it is interesting to investigate whether the toxin exploits extracellular vesicles to facilitate systemic dissemination.

To overcome technical limitations in neonatal models, we used 4-week-old mice alongside P7 neonates. The small size of P7 pups limited in vivo MRI and photoacoustic imaging, retro-orbital dye injection for BBB assessment and bone marrow sampling. Haematological profiling and peritoneal cytokine analysis were assessed in 4-week-old mice, as severe coagulopathy and limited fluid volume in toxin-exposed neonates constrained sample collection. For assays performed in parallel, findings were consistent across both age groups. Additional limitations include the need for larger multicentre cohorts to define the prevalence of Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens in NEC, and the lack of an isogenic Delta-toxin-deletion strain to further confirm Delta-toxin-dependent pathology.

Toxin-mediated injury can be initiated at a low bacterial burden and persist after bacterial clearance. Our results suggest the Delta toxin axis is a tractable precision medicine target. We developed a neutralizing monoclonal antibody that effectively blocks toxin binding, and confers protection against multi-organ damage including intestinal necrosis and brain injury. Collectively, this study suggests a subset of NEC as a toxin-driven disorder and establishes a foundation for mechanism-based therapies designed to protect the developing gut and brain.

The study involving human clinical samples was approved by the Ethics Committee of Zhujiang Hospital, Southern Medical University (2025-KY-315-02). Informed consent was obtained from all participants or their guardians. Faecal samples were collected from patients diagnosed with NEC (Bell stage II or III). For bacterial isolation, faecal specimens (0.1 g) were homogenized in 1 ml PBS, and 100 μl of the homogenate was plated onto TSC (Hopebio, HB0253) supplemented with 500 μg ml−1 d-cycloserine (Proteintech, CM01307). Plates were incubated anaerobically (80% N2, 10% H2, 10% CO2, 37 °C, 18–24 h). Single black colonies were selected and cultured in brain–heart infusion (BHI) broth (Hopebio, HB8297-1) anaerobically for 4–6 h. C. perfringens was identified by PCR amplification of the 16S rRNA gene and genes encoding the major toxins (Alpha, Beta, Epsilon, Iota, CPE, NetB, Pfo and Delta toxin).

C. perfringens isolated from faeces of patients with NEC was recovered from glycerol stock, grown overnight in BHI at 37 °C anaerobically and subcultured for 48 h to an optical density at 600 nm (OD600) of around 2.5. The culture supernatant was concentrated around 20-fold. HeLa and HT29 cells and human intestinal organoids were treated with concentrated supernatant (10 µl per 500 µl medium) for 30 min, then imaged (Olympus microscope). LDH release was measured using a commercial kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, C20301). 2% Triton X-100 was used as a 100% positive control.

Genomic DNA was extracted from faecal microbiota after overnight anaerobic culture using a magnetic bead-based kit (Tiangen, TGuide S96). The V3-V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene was amplified using primers 338F (5′-ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCA-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′). Amplicons were indexed by a second PCR using Illumina-compatible primers, pooled, size-selected by gel electrophoresis and quantified. Paired-end sequencing (2 × 250 bp) was performed on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 system. Reads were quality filtered using Trimmomatic and Cutadapt, followed by denoising, paired-end merging and chimera removal with DADA2 in R. ASVs were classified against SILVA (release 138) and UNITE (release 8.0) using BLASTn v.2.9.0 and QIIME2 Naïve Bayes (confidence threshold 0.7). Community composition and sample similarity were analysed using R packages. Sequencing data were submitted to the NCBI database (PRJNA1419495).

Bacterial DNA was extracted from pure C. perfringens isolates using the Bacterial/Fungal DNA extraction kit (magnetic beads) (Majorbio, T07-100). DNA was fragmented to about 400 bp using the Covaris M220 system, and libraries were prepared using the NEXTFLEX Rapid DNA-Seq Kit, and then processed for paired-end sequencing (2 × 150 bp) on the Illumina NovaSeq X Plus (Illumina). Raw reads were filtered with fastp (v.0.23.2) and assembled using SPAdes (v.3.15.5). The assembled genome was submitted to NCBI (PRJNA1419495). Seven genome assemblies (5 references from GenBank and 2 clinical isolates) were quality-controlled with QUAST (N50 ≥ 200 kb) and re-annotated with Prokka (v.1.14.6). Annotated sequences were clustered by OrthoSLC (v.0.2.4) for single-nucleotide polymorphism comparison. Core genes were aligned with Kalign (v.3.3.5) and concatenated into strain-specific core genomes, followed by RAxML (v.8.0.2) phylogenetic tree construction under GTRCAT with 1,000 bootstraps.

The Cd9f/f mice (T013111) were generated by GemPharmatech using CRISPR–Cas9 gene targeting technology. EllaiCre mice (T050183) and Vil1iCre mice (T004714) were purchased from GemPharmatech. Lyz2cre mice were gifted by P. Zhou. Sex- and age-matched C57BL/6 mice (both sexes; 4-week-old or neonatal) were purchased from Zhuhai BesTest Bio-Tech and randomly assigned to control or experimental groups (not blinded to investigators). Animals were bred and maintained (5 per cage) under SPF conditions with a 12 h–12 h light cycle at 22 ± 1 °C. Animal care and procedures were approved by the Ethics Committee of Guangzhou National Laboratory (GZLAB-AUCP-2024-08-A07) and followed the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. The number of mice per group was selected on the basis of previous publications.

Experimental NEC was induced in 7-day-old C57BL/6 pups (body weight: 3–3.5 g) over 4 days. Pups were gavaged every 4 h with isotonic infant formula (Similac Advance, 40 μl g−1) containing 1 × 108 CFU of C. perfringens twice daily. Age-matched controls received formula alone. Intestines were collected at P11 for histology. For antibody neutralization, neonatal mice (P0) were housed with dams until P6, then randomly assigned to five groups: (1) negative control; (2) Delta toxin+ C. perfringens (clinical 03) + isotype IgG; (3) Delta toxin+ C. perfringens (clinical 03) + anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody; (4) NCTC3181 + isotype IgG; (5) NCTC3181 + anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody. From P7 to P11, pups received a daily i.p. injection of 10 µg of the respective antibody in 50 µl sterile PBS using a 34-gauge needle. Throughout, all pups were maintained in thermoneutral cages, fed isotonic infant formula and gavaged twice daily with 1 × 108 CFU C. perfringens. At P11, pups were euthanized for tissue collection and histopathological analysis (GZLAB-AUCP-2025-05-A03). The experimental design schematic was created using BioRender (https://www.biorender.com/).

The HeLa (CCL-2), A549 (CRM-CCL-185), 5637 (HTB-9A), HEK293T (CRL-321), HT29 (HTB-38), RAW264.7 (TIB-71) and HUVEC (PCS-100-013) cell lines were obtained from ATCC. The BV2 (BGT-CMP-219) cell line was purchased from Amyjet Scientific. iBMDMs were provided by F. Shao (National Institute of Biological Sciences, Beijing)51. CD9-KO HeLa cells were obtained from T. Gallagher52. All cell lines were cultured in DMEM or RPMI-1640 medium (Gibco) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin at 37 °C with 5% CO2. All lines were confirmed to be mycoplasma free and authenticated.

Peritoneal macrophages were collected from mice by lavage with cold PBS containing 2% FBS and 1 mM EDTA. The lavage fluid was centrifuged, and the supernatant was aliquoted and stored at −80 °C for subsequent analysis. The cell pellet was resuspended in FACS buffer or complete DMEM (10% FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin). For in vitro stimulation, all purified toxins were endotoxin-depleted before incubation with macrophages.

De-identified human intestinal organoids were derived from paediatric endoscopic biopsies at Boston Children’s Hospital and provided by the Harvard Digestive Disease Center Organoid Core Facility (IRB-P00000529). Biopsies were digested with 2 mg ml−1 collagenase type I (Life Technologies, 17018029) at 37 °C for 40 min with agitation then centrifuged (500g, 4 °C, 5 min). Crypts were resuspended in Matrigel (Corning, 356231) and polymerized at 37 °C, then cultured in Matrigel with growth medium (50% L-WRN conditioned medium, 45% DMEM/F12, 1% GlutaMAX, 1% N-2/B-27, 10 mM HEPES, 100 μg ml−1 primocin/normocin, 500 nM A83-01, 500 μM N-acetyl-cysteine, 50 ng ml−1 EGF, 10 nM [Leu15]gastrin I, 10 mM nicotinamide, 10 μM SB202190; refreshed every 2 days). After 6–8 days, organoids were passaged with cell recovery solution (Corning, 354253) at 4 °C for 1 h, centrifuged, resuspended in fresh Matrigel, replated and cultured for 2 days, followed by overnight toxin treatment. Cell viability was measured using a MTT assay.

Full-length toxin genes were synthesized by Tsingke. Constructs for expressing Delta toxin, GST–Delta toxin or mutated Delta toxin (V17E/T18E) were generated by subcloning Delta toxin (residues 29–318) into the pET-22b (Addgene, 69744-3) vector with a C-terminal His6 tag or the pGEX-4T-1 (Addgene, 27458001) vector with an N-terminal GST tag.

Full-length CD9 genes from human, mouse, bovine, pig, zebrafish, chicken, Drosophila and C. elegans were synthesized by Twist Bioscience and cloned into the pcDNA3.1 vector (Invitrogen, V80020) via Gibson Assembly (NEB, E2621). Human CD9 and CD82 chimeric proteins were constructed as follows: CD9EC1CD82 (CD9(1–33)–CD82(33-53)–CD9(56–221)), CD9EC2CD82 (CD9(1–111)–CD82(111–228)–CD9(196–221)), CD9EC1EC2CD82 (CD9(1–33)–CD82(33–53)–CD9(56–111)–CD82(111–228)–CD9(196–221)), CD82EC1CD9 (CD82(1–32)–CD9(34–55)–CD82(54–250)), CD82EC2CD9 (CD82(1–110)–CD9(112–195)–CD82(229–250)), CD82EC1EC2CD9 (CD82(1–32)–CD9(34–55)–CD82(54–110)–CD9(112–195)–CD82(229–250)), with a GSGSEF linker and a triple-Flag tag at their N termini. These constructs were cloned into the pcDNA3.1 vector by Gibson Assembly. The constructs for expressing Beta toxin, Pfo or α-Hla were generated into the pET-28a vector.

Recombinant proteins (Delta toxin, Beta toxin, Pfo, α-Hla) with either a His6 or GST tag were expressed in E. coli BL21 (DE3, Thermo Fisher Scientific, EC0114) using autoinduction medium at 20 °C for 16 h. Bacterial pellets were lysed by sonication in purification buffer (200 mM NaCl, 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 10% glycerol) and clarified by centrifugation. GST-tagged proteins were purified on GSTrap columns (Cytiva, 7513101), eluted with buffer containing 10 mM reduced glutathione (Sigma-Aldrich, PHR1359), pH 7.5. His-tagged proteins were purified on HisTrap nickel columns (Cytiva, 17528601), washed with PP buffer containing 20 mM imidazole, and eluted with a linear imidazole gradient (20–500 mM). Proteins were further purified through HiTrap Q (Cytiva, 17515601) ion-exchange and HiLoad 16/60 Superdex 75 (Cytiva, 28989333) gel-filtration columns using buffer containing 200 mM NaCl, 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5. Purified proteins were concentrated and treated with an endotoxin removal kit (Beyotime, C0268). Protein concentrations were determined from measurements of absorbance at 280 nm (BioDrop spectrophotometer) using extinction coefficients calculated using the ProtParam tool (https://web.expasy.org/protparam/).

Mice received i.p. injections of Delta toxin at different doses and timepoints: 20 µg (7 days before dye injection), 100 µg (6 h before) or 1 mg LPS (6 h before). For NLRP3 inhibition, mice received a single i.p. injection of 10 mg per kg MCC950 (TargetMol, T3701) before acute Delta toxin challenge. For the chronic model, mice were i.p. administered MCC950 1 day before toxin exposure, followed by repeated administration of MCC950 every other day for 7 days. BBB permeability was assessed by retro-orbital injection of 2% Evans blue. After 2 h of circulation, mice were anaesthetized with Avertin (250 mg per kg) and transcardially perfused with PBS; the brains were dissected and photographed. For quantification, the right hemisphere was weighed, minced and incubated in 50% (w/v) trichloroacetic acid. Homogenates were centrifuged (15,000g, 30 min, 4 °C). Evans blue fluorescence was measured at 620/680 nm using the TECAN SPARK reader. The Evans blue concentration was calculated from a standard curve and normalized to brain weight. The experimental design schematic was created using BioRender (https://www.biorender.com/).

Mice received i.p. injections of 20 μg Delta toxin (7 days before imaging), 100 μg Delta toxin (4 h before imaging) or vehicle. Brain MRI was performed on a Bruker BioSpec 94/30 USR 9.4 T preclinical scanner (Bruker BioSpin MRI). T2-weighted anatomical images were acquired using a rapid acquisition with relaxation enhancement (RARE) sequence. Images were reconstructed and analysed using MicroDicom DICOM Viewer software.

Mice received i.p. injections of 20 μg Delta toxin (7 days before imaging), 100 μg Delta toxin (4 h before imaging) or vehicle. Raster scanning (10 mm × 10 mm × 2.4 mm) was performed using a small animal photoacoustic imaging system with a 532 nm pulsed laser (pulse width ≤ 8 ns, repetition rate 10 kHz, GAni, Guangzhou G-Cell Technology). Deionized water was used as the acoustic coupling medium. Photoacoustic signals were detected by a PVDF ultrasonic transducer (30 MHz centre frequency), amplified, digitized and reconstructed in real time using PAM 2.0 software (Guangzhou G-Cell Technology), with system synchronization controlled by FPGA.

Mice were anaesthetized and perfused with ice-cold PBS, followed by 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). Brains were dissected and post-fixed in 4% PFA (24 h, 4 °C), then dehydrated in 30% sucrose (in PBS) at 4 °C until saturated. Tissue was embedded in Tissue-Tek OCT compound (14020108926, Leica) and frozen on dry ice. Coronal sections (8 µm for vascular and tight junction analysis; 30 µm free-floating for microglial and astrocytic analysis) were cut using a cryostat (CM3050-S, Leica). The sections were permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100, blocked with 5% BSA, then incubated overnight at 4 °C with the following primary antibodies: ZO-1 (1:500, Invitrogen, 40-2200), IBA1 (1:1,000, Wako, 019-19741), GFAP (1:1,000, Servicebio, GB11096-50). After washing, the sections were incubated with fluorescent secondary antibodies (1 h at room temperature; Alexa Fluor 594, 1:1,000, Invitrogen, A110012; Alexa Fluor 488, 1:1,000, Invitrogen, A11008). The sections were mounted with antifade mounting medium with DAPI (Vector Labs, H-1200-10) and coverslipped. Images were acquired using the LSM800 confocal microscope (ZEISS) or a slide imaging scanner (SLIDEVIEW VS200, Evident Scientific). The ZO-1 MFI was quantified using ImageJ and normalized to the controls. IBA1 and GFAP morphologies were analysed by Imaris-based 3D reconstruction and skeletonization (Bitplane). Microglia and astrocytes were counted per field of view and normalized to cells per mm².

Single-cell suspensions from peritoneal lavage fluid, intestine and brain were filtered (70 μm) and centrifuged (400g, 5 min, 4 °C). Cells were blocked with anti-CD16/32 antibody (2.4G2, Elabscience, E-AB-F0997A) in FACS buffer on ice for 15 min. For surface marker staining, cells were incubated with fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies in FACS buffer (30 min, 4 °C). Viability was assessed using Live/Dead Fixable Violet Dead Cell Stain (Invitrogen, L34959). The following fluorescence conjugated anti-mouse CD45 (30-F11, 103112), CD4 (RM4-5, 100550), CD8 (53-6.7, 100752), CD11b (M1/70, 101210), F4/80 (BM8, 123110), Ly6G (1A8, 127606) and CD9 (MZ3,124815) antibodies were purchased from BioLegend. CD19 (1D3, 565965) was purchased from BD Biosciences. Data were collected using the BD LSRFortessa cytometer (BD Biosciences) or the SONY ID7000 Spectral Cell Analyzer, and analysed using FlowJo v.10.8.1.

Brain and intestinal tissues were dissected from anaesthetized mice and rinsed with cold PBS. For brain, single-cell suspensions were prepared using a Dounce homogenizer in RPMI 1640. For the intestine, segments were placed in Ca2+/Mg2+-free HBSS, and the mucosa was separated and incubated in a pre-digestion solution (containing 1 mM DTT and 2 mM EDTA in Ca2+/Mg2+-free HBSS) with shaking (200 rpm, 30 min, 37 °C). The intestines were washed twice with RPMI 1640 and then minced into small pieces. The digested tissues were then incubated in a digestion solution supplemented with 2 mg ml−1 collagenase IV (Yeasen, 40510ES76) and 5 U ml−1 DNase I (Sigma-Aldrich, D4263) with shaking (200 rpm, 1 h, 37 °C). Digested tissues were filtered through a 70-μm strainer (Absin, abs7306) and centrifuged (500g, 10 min, 18 °C). Immune cells were isolated by Percoll gradient centrifugation. In brief, 3 ml 30% stock isotonic Percoll (SIP; prepared as 9:1 (v/v) Percoll (Cytiva, 17089101) to 10× Ca2+/Mg2+-free HBSS) was added to the cell suspensions, layered onto 2 ml 70% SIP and centrifuged (500g, 30 min, 18 °C) with minimal/no braking. The 70–30% interphase was collected, diluted with 8 ml HBSS, centrifuged (500g, 7 min, 18 °C) and resuspended in 1 ml FACS buffer on ice.

Cells were plated in 96-well microplates overnight (around 70% confluence) and exposed to twofold serial dilutions of toxins overnight at 37 °C. MTT (0.5 mg ml−1, Research Products International, M92050) was added and incubated for 4 h at 37 °C. A total of 100 μl solubilization solution (10% SDS in 0.01 M HCl) was then added to each well and incubated overnight at room temperature. Absorbance was measured at 580 nm using a microplate reader (BMG Labtech, FLUOstar Omega). Vehicle controls were included. Viability curves were analysed using Origin software (v.8.5).

Tissue was fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin (24 h at room temperature), transferred to PBS (4 °C, 24 h), dehydrated in graded ethanol, cleared in xylene and embedded in paraffin. The sections (6 µm) were cut and stained with H&E. For intestine tissues, a well-established NEC histopathological scoring system (0 to 4) was applied: 0, no damage; 1, slight submucosal/lamina propria separation and villus tip epithelial sloughing; 2, moderate submucosal/lamina propria separation and mild villous necrosis; 3, severe submucosal/lamina propria separation, submucosal/muscular oedema and extensive villous sloughing; 4, complete villous loss and full thickness necrosis. For brain tissues, a 0–4 scale histopathological grading was performed based on the severity of neuronal damage and tissue lesions: 0, normal morphology; 1, minimal (sporadic neuronal shrinkage without structural disruption); 2, mild (focal neuronal loss in limited brain regions); 3, moderate (extensive neuronal damage with potential progression); 4, severe (diffuse neuronal necrosis involving the entire brain region examined).

Total RNA from cells was extracted with TRIzol reagent (Magen, R4801). The RNA quantity and quality were measured by NanoDrop. cDNA was synthesized from 1 μg RNA using the StarScript III One-Step RT-PCR Kit for qPCR (Genstar, A235-01). Quantitative PCR (qPCR) was performed in a 384-well format on a Real-Time PCR Detection System (Bio-Rad) using 2×RealStar Power SYBR qPCR Mix (Genstar, A311-01). Relative quantitation was performed using the \({2}^{(-\varDelta \varDelta {C}_{{\rm{T}}})}\) method using Actb (for mouse cells) for normalization. A list of the specific RT–qPCR primers is provided in Supplementary Table 3.

For serum antibody detection, 96-well plates were coated with Delta toxin (1 μg ml−1) in coating buffer (Solarbio, C1055) overnight at 4 °C. After washing in PBST, the plates were blocked with 5% BSA in PBS (1 h, room temperature) and then incubated with Delta toxin monoclonal antibody standards (1 μg ml−1, threefold serial dilution) or serum samples (starting at 1:100, threefold serial dilution) for 2 h at room temperature. After washing, HRP-conjugated goat anti-human IgG (H+L) (Yeasen, 33501ES60, 1:10,000) was added for 1 h at room temperature, followed by TMB (Solarbio, SEKF104) development and stop solution (Solarbio, SEKF101). The absorbance was measured at 450 nm (630 nm reference) using a TECAN SPARK reader. Antibody titres were determined from dilution curves.

For tissue Delta toxin quantification and distribution, tissues were weighed, homogenized in PMSF-supplemented PBS (10 μl mg−1) and subjected to three freeze–thaw cycles. After centrifugation (15,000g, 15 min, 4 °C), the supernatants were collected. The plates were coated with anti-Delta toxin mouse monoclonal antibody (1 μg ml−1) overnight at 4 °C and blocked. Serially diluted Delta toxin standards and tissue supernatants were added for 2 h at room temperature. HRP-conjugated rabbit anti-mouse IgG (H+L) (Yeasen, 771475ES60; 1: 10,000) was added for 1 h, followed by the above ELISA procedure. Tissue Delta toxin levels were normalized to uninfected controls.

Mouse IL-1β was measured using a high-sensitivity ELISA kit (ABclonal, RK04878) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Cells were lysed in RIPA buffer (Beyotime, P0013D) containing phosphatase (Roche, 4906845001) and protease inhibitors (Roche, 11836153001). Protein concentration was determined (Bio-Rad, 5000111) and normalized across samples with 20 μg protein per sample loaded. After transfer, the membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat milk in TBST (Tris-buffered saline with 0.5% Tween-20) and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies. After washing, the membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies: anti-rabbit IgG (H+L) (Proteintech, SA00001-2) and anti-mouse IgG (H+L) (Proteintech, SA00001-1). Protein bands were visualized using Clarity Western ECL substrate (SPARK, TECAN) and imaged. The following primary antibodies were used: mouse monoclonal antibodies against GST (8-326, Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA4-004), GAPDH (1E6D9, Proteintech, 60004-1-Ig); rabbit monoclonal antibody against CD9 (SA35-08, HUABIO, HA750027), tissue factor (SN20-16, HUABIO, ET1611-95), GSDMD (E9S1X, CST, 39754), NLRP3 (PSH19-43, HUABIO, HA724075), caspase 1 (1O18, Proteintech, 81482-1-RR), IL-1β (EPR16805-15, Abcam, ab234437), phospho-NF-κB p65 (Ser536) (93H1, CST, 3033), phospho-AKT (Ser473) (D9E, CST,4060), phospho-p44/42 MAPK (ERK1/2) (Thr202/Tyr204) (D13.14.4E, CST, 4370), BAX (D2E11, CST, 5023), cleaved caspase 3 (Asp175) (5A1E, CST, 9664) and β-actin (13E5, CST, 4970); and cleaved N-terminal GSDMD polyclonal antibody (Wanleibio, WL05411), cleaved-caspase 1 polyclonal antibody (Zenbio, 341030) and β-tubulin polyclonal antibody (Proteintech, 10094-1-AP).

HeLa-Cas9 cells were generated using lentiviruses (LentiCas9-Blast, Addgene, 52962) and selected using 10 µg ml−1 blasticidin S (RPI, B12150.01). The GeCKO-V2 sgRNA library was obtained from Addgene (1000000049). Sublibraries A and B were independently packed into lentiviruses. HeLa-Cas9 Cells were transduced with sgRNA lentiviral libraries at an multiplicity of infection of 0.3. Infected cells were selected with 5 µg ml−1 puromycin (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A1113830) for 1 week. Then, 3.3 × 107 cells for sublibrary A or 2.9 × 107 cells for sublibrary B were plated onto 15 cm culture dishes to ensure enough sgRNA coverage. These cells were either saved as an initial library control or exposed to 0.01 µg ml−1 Delta toxin for 24 h. The surviving cells were washed and reseeded within toxin-free medium until about 70% confluence, followed by the next round of selection with 0.01 µg ml−1 Delta toxin for 24 h. The genomic DNA of surviving cells was extracted using a commercial kit (Qiagen, 13323). The DNA fragments containing the sgRNA sequences were amplified by PCR using primers lentiGP-1_F (5′-AATGGACTATCATATGCTTACCGTAACTTGAAAGTATTTCG-3′) and lentiGP-3_R (5′-ATGAATACTGCCATTTGTCTCAAGATCTAGTTACGC-3′). Next-generation sequencing was performed by a commercial vendor (Genewiz, Illumina HiSeq). The selected sgRNA sequences (LRP6: TGGTTCTGACCGTGTAGTAT; CLEC12B: CATTGCCACATCTTAGGACA) were cloned into the LentiGuide-Puro vector (Addgene, 52963). The KO cells were generated by lentiviral transduction of sgRNAs into HeLa-Cas9 cells. Mixed populations of transduced cells were selected with puromycin (5 µg ml−1). A list of CRISPR–Cas9 screening results is provided in Supplementary Table 4.

Cells were seeded onto glass coverslips (Hampton, HR3-239). The constructs were transduced into cells for 24 h and exposed to GST-Delta toxin (0.4 μg ml−1) on ice for 60 min. After washing with cold PBS, cells were fixed with 4% PFA for 20 min, blocked with 10% goat serum for 40 min and stained with primary antibodies against GST and Flag (1:500) for 1 h, followed by fluorescence-labelled secondary antibodies for 1 h. Slides were mounted with DAPI-containing medium (SouthernBiotech, 0100-20). Images were captured using the Olympus DSU-IX81 spinning-disk confocal system, pseudocoloured and analysed using ImageJ (v.1.52o).

Cell lysates were collected in 1 ml lysis buffer (PBS, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS, plus a protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma-Aldrich), 1 ml per 10 cm dish) and incubated with 20 μg GST-tagged Delta toxin proteins for 4 h at 4 °C. Pull-down experiments were performed using 15 µl glutathione agarose beads. Beads were washed, pelleted and boiled. The samples were subjected to SDS–PAGE and western blotting. Blot images were taken using the Fuji LAS3000 imaging system and analysed using ImageJ (v.1.52o).

The binding between Delta toxin and human GST–CD9 was measured using a BLI assay with the BLItz system (ForteBio). In brief, 10 μg ml−1 biotin-labelled human GST–CD9 (Abcam, ab152262) was immobilized onto capture biosensors (GST Biosensors, ForteBio) and washed with Dulbecco’s PBS (DPBS) containing 0.5% BSA. Empty biosensors served as a control. These biosensors were then exposed to variable concentrations of Delta toxin in solution, followed by dissociation in DPBS (0.5% BSA). Binding affinities (KD) were estimated using the BLItz software (ForteBio).

Mice (BALB/c, aged 6 weeks) were immunized subcutaneously with 100 µg of purified, non-toxic mutant Delta toxin (V17E/T18E) emulsified in complete Freund’s adjuvant (CFA, Sigma-Aldrich, AR001), followed by two booster doses (50 µg in Incomplete Freund’s Adjuvant, Sigma-Aldrich, F5506) at 2-week intervals. Polyclonal antibodies were purified using protein G affinity chromatography. The final antibody titre exceeded 1:100,000 as determined by ELISA.

BALB/c mice (aged 6 weeks) were immunized subcutaneously with 100 µg of non-toxic Delta toxin mutant (V17E/T18E) in complete Freund’s adjuvant, followed by four boosters in incomplete Freund’s adjuvant. Serum titres were monitored by ELISA. Splenocytes from the highest-titre mouse were fused with SP2/0 myeloma cells. The fused cells were seeded into plates and selected in RPMI 1640-HAT medium (Sigma-Aldrich, H0262) supplemented with 10%FBS, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and gentamicin for 2 weeks. The supernatants were screened by ELISA and cytotoxicity neutralization assays to identify functional antibody-secreting clones. Positive hybridomas were subcloned by limiting dilution and amplified in RPMI 1640-HT medium (Sigma-Aldrich, H0137) supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. Stable clones were characterized by ELISA and isotyped, with one lead clone chosen for small-scale antibody purification through protein A affinity chromatography, followed by large-scale production in ascitic fluid, yielding 1 mg of purified antibody. All hybridoma lines were cryopreserved at 1 × 106 cells per vial for long-term storage.

All experiments were performed at least three times. Data are presented by descriptive statistics such as mean ± s.d. Statistical analyses were performed using the GraphPad Prism v.9.0. Statistical details of the experiments are presented in the relevant figure legends and Methods sections for each specific technique.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Data supporting the findings of this study are available within the Article and its Supplementary Information. 16S rRNA sequencing data of faeces of patients with NEC and C. perfringens genomic sequencing data were submitted to the NCBI database (PRJNA1419495). Source data are provided with this paper.

a, Stacked bar plots illustrating the high relative abundance of C. perfringens in two deceased NEC cases. b, Growth of C. perfringens in brain heart infusion (BHI) broth cultures inoculated with faecal samples from NEC patients. Turbidity indicates bacterial growth, and visible gas bubbles in C. perfringens-positive cultures confirm the characteristic gas-producing phenotype of C. perfringens, compared to a sterile blank control. c, C. perfringens strain isolation via culture on Tryptose Sulfite Cycloserine (TSC) agar. Black colonies (arrows) indicate sulfite reduction typical of C. perfringens. d, PCR validation of C. perfringens isolates via C. perfringens-specific a-toxin gene detection. e, Multiplex PCR toxin typing of clinical C. perfringens isolates. Representative gels show a Delta toxin− isolate (clinical-01) and a Delta-toxin+ isolate (clinical-03/15). Lanes denote primer sets targeting alpha-toxin (α), beta-toxin (β), epsilon-toxin (ε), iota-toxin (ι), CPE, NetB, Pfo, and delta toxin genes. f, Dot blot analysis of Delta toxin expression in the isolated clinical C. perfringens strains. Purified Delta toxin (2 μg) and culture supernatant from Delta-toxin-positive strains exhibit strong immunoreactivity with anti-Delta toxin antibody, whereas supernatant from a Delta toxin–negative strain shows no signal. g, Toxinotype classification of C. perfringens isolates based on key virulence factors34. The isolates are categorized as toxinotype C, defined by the presence of alpha and beta toxin genes, with additional detection of the delta toxin gene (red dot). h, Phylogenetic tree based on whole-genome sequencing, showing the evolutionary relationship of clinical isolates (clinical-03, clinical-01) to C. perfringens reference strains (NCTC3181, ATCC 13124, NCTC8239, NCTC8679, CVCC1160). i, j, Immunoblot analysis (i) and ELISA quantification (j) of Delta toxin in intestine, kidney, lung, and brain of neonatal mice with (n = 6) or without (n = 4) the Delta toxin+ C. perfringens infection. k, Multiplex PCR toxin typing of C. perfringens reference strains (CVCC1160, NCTC3181), confirming the presence of the delta toxin gene in NCTC3181. l, Dot blot analysis of Delta toxin expression in C. perfringens reference strains NCTC3181 and CVCC1160. m, Histopathological assessment of neonatal mice colonized with reference strains. Representative H&E sections of intestine, lung, and brain (n = 6). Compared to the mild effects of CVCC1160, NCTC3181 infection causes severe NEC-like intestinal necrosis, pulmonary septal thickening and haemorrhage, and cerebral ependymal disruption with periventricular oedema. Scale bar, 100 μm. Arrows: black, interalveolar septal thickening; green, inflammatory cell infiltration; blue, alveolar coagulation or haemorrhage (lung) or periventricular oedema (brain); brown, ependymal layer disruption, including focal detachment, vacuolization and disorganization. n, o, Representative microscopy images (n) and MTT cell viability assay (o) of HeLa cells treated with Delta toxin+ C. perfringens culture supernatant pre-incubated with either control IgG or anti-Delta toxin antibody (anti-Delta Ab). Scale bar, 50 μm. p, MTT cell viability assay of HT29 cells and human intestinal organoids treated with Delta toxin+ culture supernatant with or without neutralizing antibody. Representative images were from one of three independent experiments. Data are mean ± SD. P values determined by one-way ANOVA (o, p).

a, Survival curves of 4-week-old mice after i.p. administration of Delta toxin at the indicated doses. n = 10. b, ELISA quantification of Delta toxin in intestine, kidney, lung, and brain in Delta-toxin-treated neonatal mice (10 μg, i.p., 4 h). n = 4. c, d, Representative H&E staining (c) and histopathology scores (d) of intestine sections from control and Delta-toxin-treated 4-week-old mice (100 μg, i.p., 4 h). n = 5 (control) and n = 6 (100 μg). Scale bar, 200 μm. e, f, Histopathology scores (e) and representative coronal brain sections (f) from 4-week-old mice subjected to a single low-dose (20 μg, analysed at day 7) or acute high-dose (100 μg, analysed at 4 h) Delta toxin challenge. n = 5 (control), n = 6 (20 μg) and n = 6 (100 μg). Scale bar, 100 μm. Arrows: black, ependymal disruption; blue, periventricular vacuolation and oedema. g, Representative brain histopathology in Delta-toxin–exposed 4-week-old mice, revealing neuronal injury and oedema in the cortex. n = 6. Scale bar, 100 μm. Arrows: black, neuronal shrinkage with reduced volume and hyperchromatic cytoplasm (deeply stained), featuring indistinct nuclear–cytoplasmic boundaries; green, perivascular oedema; yellow, neuronal degeneration characterized by cytoplasmic loosening. h, Representative brain histopathology in Delta-toxin–exposed 4-week-old mice, revealing inflammatory cell infiltration in the lateral ventricle. n = 5 (control), n = 6 (20 μg) and n = 6 (100 μg). i, Histopathology scores for neuronal injury (including neuronal shrinkage and degeneration) and inflammatory cell infiltration in 4-week-old mice i.p. injected with the Delta toxin. n = 5 (control), n = 6 (20 μg) and n = 6 (100 μg). The representative histological images are shown in Extended Data Fig. 2f,g. j, k, Histopathology of the hippocampal region in Delta toxin–injected mice. n = 6 (4-week-old mice) (j) and n = 6 (neonatal mice) (k). Scale bar, 50 μm. Arrows: black, intravascular coagulation within the cerebral microvasculature. l–o, Representative histology of the renal medulla, glomerulus, and lung and quantification of coagulation pathology scores across organs of 4-week-old mice (l, m) and neonatal mice (n, o) following exposure to Delta toxin or vehicle control. n = 5. Scale bar, 100 μm. Arrows: black, coagulation or haemorrhage; green, inflammatory cell infiltration. Representative images were from one of three independent experiments. Data are mean ± SD. P values determined by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-tests (d, m, and o) and one-way ANOVA (e and i).

a, Representative photographs of mouse ear skin from control and Delta-toxin-treated 4-week-old mice (100 μg, i.p., 4 h), showing vasodilation and vascular congestion. n = 6. b, Representative images of Evans blue leakage in peritoneal lavage fluid from control and Delta-toxin-treated 4-week-old mice, indicating increased vascular permeability (100 μg, i.p., 4 h). n = 6. c, d, Haematological analysis showing polycythemia (increased RBCs) (c) and thrombocytopenia (decreased platelets) (d) in 4-week-old mice. n = 3 (control), n = 4 (20 μg, 7 d), n = 3 (100 μg, 1 h) and n = 4 (100 μg, 4 h). e–h, Coagulation assays of plasma from control and Delta-toxin-treated 4-week-old mice: Prothrombin time (PT) (e), Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT) (f), Thrombin Time (TT) (g), and Fibrinogen levels (h). The profile (prolonged PT/APTT, shortened TT, low fibrinogen) confirms a diagnosis of DIC. APTT values ≥ 200 s (upper detection limit) were recorded as 200 s. n = 3 (control), n = 4 (20 μg, 7 d), n = 3 (100 μg, 1 h) and n = 4 (100 μg, 4 h). i, Immunoblot showing Delta-toxin-induced TF release into the culture medium from RAW264.7, iBMDM, and Caco2 cells. GAPDH served as a loading control. Representative images were from one of three independent experiments. Data are mean ± SD. P values determined by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-tests (c-h).

a–c, MTT cell viability assays show that Delta toxin, but not Beta toxin, is cytotoxic to HT-29 intestinal epithelial cells (a) and intestinal organoids (b). However, Beta toxin is cytotoxic to HUVECs (c). d, Survival curves of 4-week-old mice after i.p. administration of Beta toxin at the indicated doses. n = 10. e, Representative H&E staining of the hippocampus (left) and lateral ventricle (right) of 4-week-old mice after Beta toxin challenge at various doses and times: 1 μg (analysed at day 7), 2.5 μg (analysed at 2 h), or 5 μg (analysed at 1 h). No significant histological damage was observed. n = 3. Scale bars, 1 mm (left), 200 μm (right). Representative images were from one of three independent experiments.

a, Flow cytometric analysis of the total number of CD45+ cells in brain single-cell suspensions from control and Delta-toxin-treated P7 neonates (20 μg, i.p., 4 h) and 4-week-old mice (100 μg, i.p., 4 h). n = 5. b, c, Representative flow cytometry dot plots (b) and quantification (c) of microglia frequency and absolute number in the brains of control and Delta-toxin-treated neonatal (20 μg, i.p., 4 h) and 4-week-old (100 μg, i.p., 4 h) mice. n = 5. d-g, Representative immunofluorescence images showing IBA1 (green, microglia) (d,f, top) and 3D reconstructions of IBA1+ microglia (d,f, bottom) in the hippocampus of control and Delta-toxin-treated mice. Two age groups were included: P7 neonates (20 μg, i.p., 4 h) and 4-week-old mice (100 μg, i.p., 4 h). n = 5. Quantification of microglia number is shown in (e,g, left). 3D reconstruction and morphological analysis, including total branch length, reveal a shift from ramified, resting microglia to amoeboid, activated microglia in toxin-exposed mice (e,g, right). Scale bar, 20 μm. h-k, Representative immunofluorescence images of GFAP (red, astrocytes) (h,j, top) and 3D reconstructions of GFAP+ astrocytes (i,k, bottom) in the hippocampus of control and Delta toxin-treated mice. Two age groups were included: P7 neonates (20 μg, i.p., 4 h) and 4-week-old mice (100 μg, i.p., 4 h). n = 5. Quantification of astrocyte number is shown in (i,k, left). 3D reconstructed images and the morphological parameter of volume were analysed, indicative of reactive astrogliosis (i,k, right). Scale bar, 20 μm. l, Quantification of CD4+ and CD8+ T cell proportions in CD45+ brain cells from control and Delta-toxin-treated mice. Two age groups were included: P7 neonates (20 μg, i.p., 4 h) and 4-week-old mice (100 μg, i.p., 4 h). n = 5. No significant changes were observed in T cell populations. m, Flow cytometric analysis of the total number of CD45+ cells in brain single-cell suspensions from control (n = 4) and 4 μg low-dose Delta-toxin-treated neonatal mice (n = 3), analysed at 5 days post-single injection. n, o, Representative flow cytometry dot plots (n) and quantification (o) of microglia frequency and absolute number in the brains of control (n = 4) and 4 μg low-dose Delta- toxin-treated neonatal mice (n = 3), analysed at 5 days post-single injection. p, q, Representative immunofluorescence images of IBA1 (p, green, microglia) and GFAP (q, red, astrocytes) in the hippocampus of control and Delta-toxin-treated neonatal mice (4 μg, i.p., 5 d). n = 5. r, Quantification of microglia number and astrocyte immunofluorescence intensity in the hippocampus of control and Delta-toxin-treated neonatal mice. n = 5. s, t, Representative flow cytometry dot plots (s) and quantification (t) of CD4+ and CD8+ T cell proportions in CD45+ brain cells from control (n = 4) and 4 μg low-dose Delta-toxin-treated neonatal mice (n = 3), analysed at 5 days post-single injection. Representative images were from one of three independent experiments. Data are mean ± SD. Statistical analysis was performed using two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-tests (a, c, e, g, i, k, l, m, o, r and t).

a, Schematic of the experimental design for the Evans blue assay to evaluate BBB integrity by Delta toxin or LPS in 4-week-old mice with or without the NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950. b, Gating strategy for flow cytometry analysis of peritoneal immune cells. c, d, Representative flow cytometry dot plots (c) and quantification (d) of peritoneal macrophages (CD11b+Ly6G−) and neutrophils (CD11b+Ly6G+) in single-cell suspensions from 4-week-old mice peritoneal lavage fluid. n = 5 (control), n = 4 (100 μg, 1 h), n = 5 (100 μg, 4 h) and n = 5 (20 μg, 7 d). e, f, Representative flow cytometry dot plots (e) and quantification (f) of intestinal immune cells of neonatal mice, analysed at 4 h after i.p. injection of 20 μg Delta toxin or vehicle control. n = 4. g, Immunoblot analysis of NLRP3 and caspase-1 cleavage in iBMDMs treated with a sublytic dose of Delta toxin (5 ng mL−1) in the presence or absence of 40 mM extracellular KCl for 8 h. Representative images were from one of three independent experiments. Data are mean ± SD. Statistical analysis was performed using one-way ANOVA (d), two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-tests (f). The diagram in a was created using BioRender; Zhang, S. https://BioRender.com/o2lct20 (2026).

a, HeLa, A549, 5637, 293 T, and HT29 cells were exposed to serial dilutions of Delta toxin for 4 h. Cell viability was measured by MTT assays. b, WT HeLa and UGCG-KO cells were exposed to serial dilutions of Delta toxin for 4 h. Cell viability was measured using MTT assays. c, HeLa cells were exposed to serial dilutions of Delta toxin for 4 h in the presence or absence of EtDO-P4. Cell viability was measured using MTT assays. d, Mixed stable CLEC12B or LRP6-KO HeLa cells were generated using CRISPR-Cas9. These KO cells and the control WT cells were exposed to serial dilutions of Delta toxin for 4 h, and cell viability was measured using MTT assays. e, f, Representative BLI sensorgrams of different concentrations of Delta toxin (e) and kinetic parameters (f) of Delta toxin binding to CD9.

a, Immunostaining analysis showed that 3xFLAG insertions into the CD9 EC1 domain do not disrupt toxin binding. Nuclei were labelled with DAPI. Scale bar, 10 μm. b, Domain swapping confirmed the EC2 domain is required for binding. Immunostaining analysis showed that GST-tagged Delta toxin (red) bound to cells overexpressing chimeric proteins (FLAG-positive, green) containing the CD9 EC2 domain. Nuclei were labelled with DAPI (blue). Scale bar, 10 μm. c, 3x FLAG-tagged H. sapiens, M. musculus, B. taurus, S. scrofa, D. rerio, G. domestics, Drosophila, and C. elegans CD9 were expressed in HeLa CD9-KO cells (immunostained with anti-FLAG Alexa-488). #1343. Aston Villa threatening Jamie Carragher with legal action over 'insults' looks wild... but this is why club's billionaire owner Nassef Sawiris has had enough, writes TOM COLLOMOSSE

Published: 07:00 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 08:54 EDT, 31 October 2026

Before billionaires Nassef Sawiris and Wes Edens took control of Aston Villa in summer 2018, the club were staring into the abyss.

Villa had just lost the Championship play-off final to Fulham and facing another year without Premier League funds, the club’s financial future was uncertain.

Eight years later, Villa have qualified for the Champions League for the second year in three. In Unai Emery, they have one of the world’s best coaches.

Despite significant issues navigating Premier League and UEFA financial rules, they lifted the Europa League last season and look well-equipped to challenge for a top-five finish again this term. In Sawiris’ time, they have made two £100million sales – Jack Grealish to Manchester City for £100m in 2021, and Morgan Rogers to Chelsea for £117m last summer, while investing hugely in players and making Emery one of the world’s best-paid coaches. Villa are also taking the capacity of Villa Park past 50,000.

By any measure, this is a club on the rise and Sawiris should feel very proud of what they have achieved during his tenure.

So you can imagine his irritation when Emery, the club’s most valuable asset, is being pushed towards the Manchester United job by a high-profile pundit like Jamie Carragher, apparently because Villa is not big enough for him. That said, the post that landed on Villa’s X account at 10.16pm on Friday still took the breath away.

Aston Villa is a club on the rise and Sawiris (above) should feel very proud of what they have achieved during his tenure

Jamie Carragher has been pushing Unai Emery towards the Manchester United job on The Overlap podcast, claiming that Villa 'will never be' United (source: TheOverlap/YouTube)

‘Aston Villa will initiate legal action against Jamie Carragher for his unacceptable insults about the Club and its fans.

‘Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football. Nassef Sawiris, Chairman.’

It is unclear which ‘insults’ drove Sawiris to this step. Carragher has talked up Emery’s candidacy for United on different platforms and received the inevitable backlash from Villa supporters online. Carragher doubled down on his view on The Overlap podcast this week, in which he told ‘Aston Villa fans’ to ‘shut the f*** up.’

He continued: ‘But the reason I’m going to go back at Villa fans is I can’t believe that a manager who is so successful in the Europa League, take a player, if you’d won the Europa League three or four times (Emery has won it five times) surely you’ll then want to go for the Champions League.

‘Aston Villa will never be Manchester United. I just think he didn’t do well at PSG or Arsenal, and maybe that’s because of egos in the dressing room and that sort of thing.

'But surely he would want that opportunity to manage a giant again. There is a chain in football, whether you like it or not.’

The former Liverpool and England defender eventually apologised for his comments on Saturday, writing on Twitter: 'I’d like to apologise to Aston Villa, the owners & their fans. My language this week was clumsy & wrong.

'I can assure Villa fans it was tongue in cheek but I can understand it’s not come across that way, so apologies. Good luck today UTV!'

Villa have been mocked for this response but look at it from their point of view. The club feel that at every turn, the established order are trying to slow their progress. Consider the financial regulations that favour traditionally wealthy clubs who make money off the pitch, over those who succeed on it.

Imagine the frustration of finishing fourth in the Premier League, winning the Europa League and then having to sell six starters from the final.

Last season Villa finished fourth in the Premier League, won the Europa League and then had to sell six of their starters from the final

Threatening legal action against a pundit may look wild but it does not come from a clear blue sky. Like many of the billionaire class, Sawiris is a tough operator and has taken an increasingly hands-on role at Villa in recent years.

He drove the move to hire Emery in 2022 and he has been more and more involved in transfers. He has forged good, professional relations with some of football’s other key players, including super-agent Jorge Mendes and Chelsea chief Behdad Eghbali. Sawiris ensured Villa received a record fee for Rogers and he was also instrumental in the capture of 18-year-old winger Ibrahim Mbaye from Paris Saint-Germain last summer. His ambition for Villa is limitless.

For seasons now, Villa have operated in what Sawiris may feel is an arbitrary financial straitjacket. Now he has to listen to ex-players with significant influence telling the world that Villa can never satisfy Emery’s ambition.

Carragher is probably guilty of nothing more than expressing an opinion, however crudely he may have done so. But if Sawiris is fed up of various voices and organisations trying to put Villa back in their box, then who can blame him?
