#1342. Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Models of early human dispersal rely on climate to predict where populations could settle, with freshwater assumed to govern the timing and geography1,2, particularly across the Saharo-Arabian arid belt, where humid windows episodically opened corridors into the desert interior3. Yet Pleistocene dispersals into ‘Green Arabia’ were brief and geographically constrained4,5, a pattern not explained by water availability alone. Here we show, from an approximately 1,500-km geoarchaeological survey through the Rub’ al Khali of Arabia, the largest sand sea in the world, that the availability of stone for tool manufacture operated as an independent factor on early human settlement. Palaeolake deposits were recorded at 55 of 125 localities investigated, yet no lithic artefacts and no knappable raw materials were found along the transect, with ground-surface visibility exceeding 95%, despite abundant freshwater and contemporary occupation at the desert margins. Spatial modelling of the Peninsula supports the inference that settlement tracked the co-occurrence of water and lithic raw materials rather than water alone. Across the Peninsula, 57% of water-accessible terrain lies on formations that lack knappable stone and adding raw-material availability raises discrimination of known site locations from an area under the curve of 0.695 to 0.768. Convergent patterns from Africa, North America and Asia indicate that the constraint is not peculiar to Arabia. Dispersal models that omit raw-material geology may systematically overestimate the habitable range of stone-tool-dependent populations.

Predictive models of early human dispersal across Arabia, built primarily on palaeohydrological reconstructions of palaeolake and palaeoriver networks and on climate-envelope reconstructions of precipitation and net primary productivity, identify interior basins as high-probability zones for Middle Palaeolithic (MP) and Middle Stone Age (MSA) occupation3,6, the broadly contemporaneous prepared-core industries of western Eurasia and Africa, respectively; because Arabian assemblages show affinities with both, the joint term MP/MSA is used throughout. The expectation that these palaeolakes attracted human settlement reflects decades of palaeoclimatic research demonstrating that orbital forcing periodically transformed the Arabian Peninsula into landscapes of lakes, wetlands and grasslands7,8,9. Geographical Information System (GIS)-based models built on this record have shown predictive success at the Rub’ al Khali margins, where dated MP/MSA assemblages occur alongside lacustrine deposits in the western basin10,11. Yet these models have never been verified against systematic ground survey in the desert interior, nor have they been evaluated against the distribution of knappable raw materials, a resource fundamental to Palaeolithic subsistence12 and consumed at rates that varied with the technology used13,14. Although it has been recognized that water would not be the sole determining factor in site location6, no study has evaluated this other variable.

The Rub’ al Khali occupies around 650,000 km2 of the southern Arabian Peninsula, bounded by the Asir and Yemen highlands to the west, the Dhofar Nejd and Hadhramaut plateaus to the south, the Hajar Mountains to the east and the Tuwaiq escarpment and Ad Dahna desert to the north. Its interior is dominated by longitudinal dune systems separated by interdunal corridors in which Quaternary sediments are exposed by deflation. During Pleistocene humid intervals, precession-driven intensification of the Indian Ocean monsoon raised regional water tables and formed lakes across the basin7,8,9,15, the most extensive of which are documented for Marine Isotope Stage 516. Archaeological evidence for these intervals is concentrated at the desert margins, where MP/MSA assemblages occur alongside dated lacustrine deposits at Mundafan10,11, Jebel Faya17,18, Umm al Sha’al19 and the Dhofar Nejd Plateau5,20. These assemblages are technologically diverse: Levallois and other prepared-core reduction strategies predominate, with Nubian Levallois industries of African affinity documented in the south20,21 and assemblages of western Asian character in the north4. The interior basin itself, however, has never been surveyed systematically and its archaeological status has been inferred from the margins rather than tested.

To test the prediction that interior basins were high-probability zones for MP/MSA occupation, a systematic geoarchaeological reconnaissance of the desert interior was conducted along an approximately 1,500-km transect through the central Rub’ al Khali (Fig. 1). The survey targeted palaeolake deposits correlated to sections independently dated to about 122,000–67,000  years ago16, focusing on the MP/MSA. This period corresponds to both the dated palaeolake chronologies and documented Homo sapiens dispersals into Arabia17,20,22. Because the nearest known knappable outcrops lie more than 200 km from the surveyed basins, the interior decouples water from stone. This study therefore tests whether the co-occurrence of freshwater and knappable stone, rather than freshwater alone, accounts for the distribution of archaeologically visible MP/MSA occupation in the Arabian interior. If freshwater alone governed settlement, MP/MSA populations occupying the adjacent margins would be expected to have left archaeologically visible traces in the interior during humid phases. Abundant evidence for palaeolakes was recorded, but no knappable raw materials, no lithic artefacts and no trace of human occupation were found. An independent spatial model, validated against 301 MP/MSA findspots in adjacent Oman, indicates that settlement was concentrated in zones where both water and raw materials co-occurred; a Peninsula-wide analysis shows the same pattern across 363 documented MP/MSA sites.

a, Rub’ al Khali crossing expedition track (black line) shows the survey transect. Red filled circles indicate dated MP/MSA sites with published chronometric ages surrounding the study area; these are sites whose chronologies are plotted in b. Blue filled circles indicate surveyed localities where palaeolake evidence was recorded (n = 55); black open circles indicate localities lacking palaeolake indicators (n = 70). Blue open diamonds mark published palaeolake localities7,16. Sand dune extent defined by Quaternary aeolian deposit boundaries62; Rub’ al Khali corresponds to the continuous sand sea labelled in the south-central Peninsula. b, Published optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) chronologies for central interior palaeolakes16 (blue; n = 7 determinations from five sections) and dated MP/MSA sites at the basin margins (red; n = 21 determinations from seven sites). Grey vertical bands mark Marine Isotope Stage substages, labelled at the top. Error bars show ±1σ analytical uncertainty on each individual age determination; no statistics are derived across determinations. Numeric ages (kyr, thousand years) for archaeological sites presented in Supplementary Table 4. Scale bar, 300 km. Coastlines and national boundaries in a from Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com).

Human occupation potential across the Arabian Peninsula was modelled from mapped surface geology and reconstructed drainages. This dual-resource model was initially tested in Oman, where systematic survey allowed for estimating the likelihood of raw-material availability. The model shows that occupation potential is concentrated in narrow zones where both water and knappable raw materials co-occur, predominantly along the Dhofar Nejd and western Hajar piedmont, whereas interior regions score low despite their proximity to water (Extended Data Fig. 1c). Known MP/MSA sites cluster overwhelmingly in these highest-potential zones (Extended Data Fig. 1d), consistent with settlement tracking the co-occurrence of water and knappable stone, rather than water alone (Supplementary Fig. 7). The same pattern emerges at the Peninsula-wide scale (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 2); of the total area of the Arabian Peninsula within water-proximity thresholds, 57% lies on geological formations that lack knappable lithologies.

a, Dual-resource model for the Arabian Peninsula. A total 57% of the area classified as water accessible lacks knappable raw material and is excluded from the dual-resource model. Small red dots indicate MP/MSA sites. b, Statistical validation: proportions of published MP/MSA sites (n = 362 of 363 compiled sites in the modelled extent; solid red line) across discrete modelled human occupation potential, compared with the median (blue dashed line) and 2.5th to 97.5th percentile range (blue shading) of 999 simulations under a spatially random null distribution. Sites are significantly over-represented in zones of highest modelled potential (3) and significantly under-represented in zones where neither resource occurs (0), with observed proportions falling outside the 95% envelope of the Monte Carlo simulations. The subset of known sites in low-potential zones is the expected consequence of the conservative binary classification of the Peninsula raw-material layer, under which formations bearing localized siliceous occurrences not captured at 1:2,000,000 resolution are recorded as lacking stone. Coastlines and national boundaries in a from Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com).

The expedition investigated 125 localities along the survey transect, of which 55 yielded palaeolake deposits (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). The eastern localities lie among sections independently dated by luminescence to Marine Isotope Stage 5, between about 122 thousand years ago (ka) and 67 ka (ref. 16). Contemporary occupation is documented at the Rub’ al Khali margins at Mundafan (about 96–77 ka)10,11, Umm al Sha’al (about 87–71 ka)19, Jebel Faya (about 134–80 ka)17,18,23 and the Dhofar Nejd plateau (about 109–95 ka)5,20 (Fig. 1b, Supplementary Table 4 and Supplementary Information, section 6). Freshwater lakes and nearby populations therefore seem to have overlapped regionally across this interval, yet the surveyed interior produced no archaeologically visible occupation evidence. Carbonate lacustrine sediments, ostrich eggshell fragments, and freshwater mollusc assemblages dominated by Melanoides tuberculata and Corbicula fluminalis were observed at palaeolake localities (Fig. 3). Sedimentological features, including bioturbated limestones, dolomitic microbial build-ups, gypsum rosettes indicative of terminal desiccation and trace fossils characteristic of shallow lacustrine environments, are consistent with previous palaeoenvironmental interpretations. These waterbodies ranged from freshwater at highstand, indicated by the mollusc and limestone facies, to saline during desiccation. More localities were recorded at equivalent elevations to the deposits investigated by ref. 16 and represent fragmented remnants of the same palaeolake systems (Extended Data Fig. 3 and Supplementary Information, section 3).

a, Partly exposed stratified palaeolake deposit of bioturbated sandstone and claystone, site 116; sabkha evaporites mixed with aeolian sands in the foreground. b, M. tuberculata molluscs in situ, site 52. c, Massive carbonate platform more than 20-cm thick, strongly bioturbated and with abundant M. tuberculata gastropods, site 52. d, Polygonal gypsiferous laminated dolomitic microbial build-ups, site 80. e, C. fluminalis bivalves and ostrich eggshell fragment, site 45. Scale bars, 6 m (a), 15 cm (b), 15 cm (c), 50 cm (d) and 15 cm (e). Geotagged photographs are archived by locality identifier in the OSF repository (https://osf.io/4mw23).

The transect started at isolated outcrops of Jurassic Hanifa Formation, which provided lithic raw material for the MP/MSA occupation at nearby Mundafan10,11. Approximately 80 km further northeast, the last bedrock outcrops were documented (Lower Cretaceous Wasia Formation); these yielded heavily weathered silicified sandstones, of limited suitability for stone tool manufacture (sites 8 and 9; Supplementary Information, section 1). East of these outcrops, the chert-bearing Mesozoic–Eocene formations dip beneath a thick sequence of Miocene to Quaternary siliciclastic, carbonatic and evaporitic sediments. In the central Rub’ al Khali, only small, isolated remnants of these younger basin-fill deposits are exposed between dune fields and none contains knappable lithologies (Fig. 4). Despite systematic reconnaissance and high ground visibility, no lithic artefacts or other cultural materials were recorded at any surveyed locality and no lithic raw materials were found throughout the transect, whether as exposed bedrock or transported clasts, except at its westernmost and easternmost ends. Knappable stone was confined to 10 of 125 localities (8%): two Wasia Formation outcrops in the west and eight eastern-margin localities comprising one Dammam Formation bedrock exposure and seven alluvial gravel deposits carrying reworked chert. No lithic artefacts were recovered at these localities either. Across the intervening around 800 km of interior basin, surface lithologies consist exclusively of carbonatic, evaporitic and siliciclastic facies, none of which possesses the conchoidal fracture properties required for stone tool manufacture (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Information, section 1).

a, Surface geology classified by the presence or absence of knappable lithologies (chert, quartzite, quartz, chalcedony, silicified limestone or sandstone and rhyolite), based on the US Geological Survey (USGS) geological map of the Arabian Peninsula62,63 with raw-material classifications from published formation descriptions63. Quaternary aeolian sand is shown separately, as it obscures the underlying bedrock rather than representing a distinct lithological class. Main surface exposures of the formations named in the text are labelled. Black open circles show survey localities from the Rub’ al Khali crossing expedition where no lithic raw material was observed (n = 115); blue filled circles show localities where knappable raw material was present (n = 10), all restricted to the western and eastern basin margins. Red dots indicate the full compilation of documented MP/MSA sites used in the spatial analysis (n = 363; localities outside the mapped extent are not shown). The dashed line approximates the transect shown in b. b, Schematic geological cross-section along the survey transect, illustrating the burial of Palaeocene–Eocene chert-bearing formations beneath Neogene and Quaternary basin fill across the Rub’ al Khali interior. Serrated ornament along the ground surface denotes the extent of the active sand sea. The Dammam Formation is not differentiated in the source section; the arrow marks the position along the transect at which it crops out. The formations traversed by the section are named in b; the geological colour scheme is common to both a and b. Structural and stratigraphic relationships are modified after ref. 30 and expedition field observations. The vertical exaggeration is approximately ×120. Scale bars, 300 km (a) and 200 km (b). Coastlines and national boundaries in a from Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com).

Collectively, these results indicate that the central basin of the Rub’ al Khali produced no archaeologically visible evidence of occupation throughout the MP/MSA, despite (1) the abundance of freshwater lakes, (2) the presence of contemporary human occupations around the desert margins (Fig. 1b) and (3) the demonstrated capacity of MP/MSA populations for long-distance lithic transport24,25,26,27,28. Ground visibility exceeded 95% across deflationary interdunal surfaces and the identification of centimetre-scale gastropods and ostrich eggshell fragments suggests that lithic artefacts would have been conspicuous had they been present. Nor can the vacancy be attributed to a reliance on perishable technologies in place of stone. Organic implements are themselves manufactured and maintained with lithic tools, so any resident toolkit would have generated the durable debris of edge production and resharpening. The same populations, moreover, left abundant lithic assemblages wherever knappable stone was available at the desert margins. Future fieldwork may yet document small logistical or procurement sites in the interior but, against a systematic pattern of absence across 55 palaeolake localities spanning the full transect, such finds would represent low-intensity events rather than evidence of sustained settlement.

This absence reflects the surface geology of the central basin, which is composed exclusively of carbonate and evaporite formations lacking cryptocrystalline silicate lithologies suitable for stone tool manufacture29,30. Interior palaeolakes were fed by groundwater rather than surface runoff, as indicated by fine-grained lacustrine sediments lacking coarse clastic input (Supplementary Information, section 2). Permanent lakes persist in the Rub’ al Khali interior today, fed exclusively by artesian groundwater31 and Nefud palaeolakes were similarly groundwater-fed systems without surface connectivity32. Unlike river-fed lakes, groundwater-fed systems have no fluvial mechanism to transport knappable stone from distant sources.

The vacancy is not confined to the MP. The interior was extensively rewatered during the Early Holocene humid phase, with perennial lakes and river systems reforming across the Rub’ al Khali33, yet the central basin surveyed here yielded no cultural material of any period, Lower Palaeolithic, MP or Holocene. Holocene occupation concentrated instead in the oasis basins and interdune playas of the Nefud to the north34 and on the northern margin the few reported Neolithic traces take the form of ephemeral hearth scatters that remain largely uninvestigated35. Where mobile pastoralists occupied these northern basins, they provisioned their toolkits from small clasts, importing finer raw material from distant and unknown sources and left no structural remains, only lightweight and ephemeral camps35. The southern margin, where knappable stone crops out locally, records a different outcome. At Maitan, on the incised Eocene limestone plateau at the southern edge of the sand sea, Dammam Formation flint nodules occur in the surveyed area and are the probable source of the local industry, alongside finer flint drawn from outcrops of the same formation tens to hundreds of kilometres distant. High artefact densities and grinding equipment indicate recurrent occupation during the Holocene humid phase, although no architectural features were recorded36. This persistence of absence across climatically distinct humid phases supports the inference that raw-material availability, rather than water, was the limiting factor on archaeologically visible occupation.

Occupation around the Jubbah palaeolake in northern Saudi Arabia provides the positive counterpart. Like the Rub’ al Khali basins, Jubbah is an interior palaeolake system isolated from regional drainage. Unlike the Rub’ al Khali, however, it sits on Saq Sandstone that supplied locally abundant quartzite and MP populations occupied its shorelines37,38. The Duqm region of central Oman provides the inverse: chert is abundant and of comparable quality to the Dhofar Nejd, yet MP/MSA sites are rare39, a pattern attributed to the scarcity of freshwater40. Where the Rub’ al Khali has water without stone, Duqm has stone with little water and archaeological site density is very low in both cases. The same asymmetry appears in the transect itself: the ten localities at which knappable stone was recorded, all at the basin margins, likewise yielded no artefacts, indicating that the presence of stone alone was no more sufficient than the presence of water alone. On the Dhofar Nejd, MSA populations occupied chert-rich landscapes during Marine Isotope Stage 5c but occupation appears to have ceased when freshwater failed during Marine Isotope Stage 5b, despite continued access to raw material5. In each case, settlement tracks the co-occurrence of water and knappable stone; where either resource is missing, occupation is rare or absent. The two resources are only weakly correlated across the model domain (Pearson’s r = −0.15), so their joint distribution is not reducible to a single underlying variable such as piedmont setting or drainage incision, because a shared geomorphological control would produce covariance between them and none is present.

The observation that the availability of knappable stone influences settlement independently of water is not unique to Arabia. On the Messak Plateau of Libya, 91% of MSA occurrences concentrate near quartzarenite outcrops despite abundant water across adjacent lowlands41. On the Tibetan Plateau, Terminal Pleistocene occupation was governed by the localized availability of gneissic pebbles at glacial meltwater confluences, the only knappable material in a granite-dominated landscape42. In the Eastern Desert of Egypt, MSA sites are associated strictly with specific sandstone formations and are absent from water-rich but lithic-poor areas43. At Taramsa in the Egyptian Nile Valley and Jojosi in South Africa, MSA groups made repeated, specialized visits to single raw-material outcrops, ignoring other locally available lithologies to export prepared blanks across the wider landscape44,45. In eastern North America, Clovis Palaeoindian settlement systems seem to have been centred around stone outcrops, with raw-material sources functioning as the hubs around which subsistence strategies were organized46. These convergent patterns, across different geological substrates, hydrological regimes and chronological contexts, provide analogical support for a ‘tethering’ effect whereby stone-tool-dependent populations become tied to raw-material sources47. In most of these settings water was widely available, so the distribution of knappable stone alone structured settlement. Arabia represents the more constrained case in which both resources were patchy and occupation required their co-occurrence. The prepared-core technologies that dominated Arabian MP/MSA assemblages sharpened this dependence further, because they consumed substantial raw material in core preparation10,11,23,48.

The Arabian Peninsula seems to have comprised a patchwork of discrete zones where water and lithic raw materials co-occurred, attracting and sustaining MP/MSA settlement. Existing dispersal models prioritize topographic variables, climate and water availability1,2,3,49,50 but do not incorporate lithic resource distributions. Although MP/MSA populations could transport stone over long distances24,26,28, the quantities moved decline steeply with distance. In well-documented MP systems, most raw material in an assemblage (60–98% by frequency) derives from sources within about 5 km, whereas sources beyond 20–30 km rarely contribute more than 5% and usually 1–2% (ref. 51). In western Europe about 100 km represents a characteristic upper threshold on transfer, and in central Europe, where the longest recorded distances reach 300 km, transfers at that range account for 7 of 100 recorded occurrences and exceed 1% of an assemblage in only three cases51. Neutral models of embedded procurement reproduce such distances from ordinary foraging mobility at three to four times the foraging radius, without invoking deliberate provisioning or exchange52,53.

Occasional acquisition and sustained provisioning are distinguished not by distance alone but by the technological stage at which material arrives. Locally procured stone enters sites as nodules or roughed-out blocks and is reduced on the spot, with all stages of the reduction sequence represented. Material from beyond 20 km arrives as blanks or finished tools, heavily resharpened, with the final stages of reduction overrepresented51. The first signature indicates a resident lithic economy, the second occasional acquisition embedded in wider mobility. Sustained occupation of the Rub’ al Khali interior would require the first, across more than 200 km between disconnected groundwater-fed lakes with no intermediate sources. Where MP settlement was drawn to water on stone-poor ground it operated at a far smaller scale: at Kůlna in Moravia, occupied for its mineral springs rather than its lithic resources, local material contributes only 1–3% of the assemblage and the nearest silicate source lies 10 km away, a distance covered in a single day51. Such long-range acquisition can furnish occasional pieces, but it cannot supply the daily tool production of a resident population over generations.

The dual-resource pattern observed here need not have a single cause. If MP/MSA populations entering Arabia were small, as might be expected of foragers colonizing unfamiliar territory54,55, settlement in favourable zones may never have generated the demographic pressure required to push groups into neighbouring regions lacking essential resources, so that populations were drawn into dual-resource zones rather than forced out of them56. Landscape knowledge would have reinforced the same tendency, because foragers accumulate and transmit detailed environmental knowledge over generations57,58 and awareness that the interior lacked knappable stone may itself have functioned as a deterrent59,60. Terrain roughness has been proposed as an influence on habitat selection, because rugged landscapes juxtapose ecotones and so support higher biome diversity and a wider range of foods61. Arabian MP/MSA sites do occupy somewhat rougher ground than background locations, although the effect is small (Cliff’s delta = 0.197) and roughness runs inversely to the distribution of knappable stone across the Peninsula (Spearman’s rho = −0.217), knappable lithologies occurring disproportionately on low-relief terrain, so it cannot generate the observed association and adds no discriminatory power to the dual-resource model (Extended Data Fig. 4). The ecological mechanism itself cannot be tested against the palaeoproductivity record presently available for Arabia. The demographic and landscape-learning processes would have operated together with the targeting of dual-resource areas, concentrating MP/MSA populations in favourable zones rather than in the resource-poor interior (Supplementary Information, section 7). Whatever their relative contribution, the consequence is the same, in that populations occupying northern and central Arabia and those in the south would have experienced limited demographic exchange across the archaeologically vacant interior.

Incorporating raw-material geology substantially reduces the area suitable for settlement. Thus, when raw-material geology is factored into existing climate-based models, more than half the area conventionally classified as habitable was of low potential for sustained MP/MSA occupation under the dual-resource model. This figure is conservative, because formations were counted as raw-material-bearing wherever any knappable lithology is documented, whether or not it is available at the surface across their mapped extent, so the water-accessible area lacking usable stone is unlikely to be smaller than 57%. At the 1:2,000,000 resolution of the source geology and given the binary nature of the raw-material classification, the estimate is necessarily approximate, but the qualitative result, that a substantial majority of the water-accessible Peninsula lacks knappable stone, is not sensitive to it. This correction extends beyond Arabia to any arid landscape on which early humans settled.

These results indicate that ‘Green Arabia’ was a lithic archipelago whose islands were defined as much by geology as by climate; dispersal models that omit lithic raw-material distributions may systematically overestimate the area habitable by stone-tool-dependent populations. For Pleistocene arid landscapes, the viable territory was not merely where water occurred, but the fraction of those areas where water and knappable stone coincided. This fraction was not fixed, however, but would have varied with how much raw material a given tool technology consumed13,14. The settlement patterns documented here are consistent with populations tethered to raw-material sources. More economical reduction systems, or composite technologies that extend the working life of a small amount of stone, may later have eased that dependence, although this lies beyond the record examined here48. This dependence governed not only where people settled but how far they could spread, with dispersal advancing between dual-resource islands and stalling where those islands lay beyond reach of one another5,40. Whether early human populations settled a desert landscape depended as much on the stone exposed across its surface as on the water that filled its basins.

Artificial intelligence (AI) tools (Claude and Gemini) were used to assist with paper preparation, including editing for clarity and style. AI was also used to assist with the development of R code for spatial analysis and figure preparation. All scientific content, analytical design, interpretation and conclusions are the sole responsibility of the authors, who have verified all analytical outputs and take full responsibility for the accuracy of the work. Fieldwork in the Rub’ al Khali, Saudi Arabia, consisted strictly of non-invasive, non-collecting surface reconnaissance. Before the expedition, the research team engaged with the Saudi Ministry of Culture to coordinate activities. Because the proposed approximately 1,500-km continuous transect was unprecedented in scale and designed purely as an observational survey, the Ministry advised that site-specific archaeological research permits were not applicable. Consequently, no excavation was undertaken and no artefacts, sediments, rock samples or biological specimens were collected or removed from Saudi Arabia. All observations were recorded in situ using photography and Global Positioning System (GPS) logging. Fieldwork in Oman was conducted under permits issued by the Ministry of Heritage and Tourism, in the framework of collaborative research programmes initiated in 2002. A subset of the Omani site data was derived from commercial Environmental Impact Assessments conducted by J.I.R., undertaken in compliance with Omani heritage legislation (RD 2019-35) and IFC Performance Standard 8. All data and analytical code have been made public in an online repository.

The Rub’ al Khali crossing expedition team conducted systematic geoarchaeological reconnaissance along an approximately 1,500-km transect through the central Rub’ al Khali between 15 November and 20 December 2023 (35 days). Route length was measured from the continuous GPS track recorded throughout the traverse and archived with the survey documentation; the straight-line distance between the western and eastern termini is about 1,070 km. The expedition comprised eight team members using three purpose-built expedition vehicles equipped with fuel, water (about 1,700 litres) and supplies enabling six weeks of autonomous operation. Route planning involved analyzing satellite imagery to chart a passage through the dune fields (Google Earth, Sentinel-2), targeting the palaeolake belt documented by ref. 16, in which several sections had been independently dated by luminescence.

Localities were identified through satellite imagery analysis, searching for visible lacustrine deposits and published palaeolake locations. Survey strategy comprised systematic pedestrian reconnaissance within corridors of about 500-m radius centred on exposed lacustrine sediments. Time allocated per locality varied from 10 min to 5 h depending on exposure extent and accessibility. Survey corridors totalled around 43 km2 of systematically reconnoitred area (calculated as π × (0.5 km)2 per locality × 55 palaeolake localities). Combined with more than 95% ground-surface visibility, this represents survey intensity comparable to published regional investigations. Surface facies and terrain were classified in the field by direct observation, following standard geological criteria for lacustrine, evaporitic, fluvial-alluvial and aeolian depositional environments; determinations were made by a field geologist (R.W.D.) at each locality and recorded photographically. Facies definitions and their distribution along the transect are given in Supplementary Information, section 1.

Survey targets included (1) lithic artefacts or manufacturing debris, (2) mollusc shells, (3) ostrich eggshell fragments, (4) sedimentary features characteristic of lacustrine environments, (5) trace fossils and (6) lithic raw materials suitable for stone tool manufacture. Malacological identifications were made exclusively from field photographs. This is a methodological limitation, because assemblage composition is more informative than the presence or absence of individual taxa and the identifications should be treated as indicative rather than definitive (Supplementary Information, section 8). Geographic coordinates were recorded using GPS (±5–10-m accuracy). All features were photographed with GPS geotagging. Aerial documentation used drone photography. No physical samples were collected.

The Oman dataset derives from 44 archaeological survey campaigns conducted between 2002 and 2024 across six governorates (Dhofar, Ad Dakhliyah, Al Wusta, Adh Dhahirah, Ash Sharqiyah and Musandam), comprising 13 research campaigns, 27 environmental impact assessment surveys and four reconnaissance surveys (Supplementary Table 3 and Supplementary Information, section 4). Coverage encompassed diverse geological and hydrological contexts, including mountain piedmont, plateau, escarpment, interior gravel plain and sand sea settings and recorded both localities at which archaeological material or knappable raw material was present and localities at which neither occurred. This combination of positive and null observations provides the empirical basis for the raw-material probability model. At each locality, the presence or absence of knappable lithic raw material was recorded alongside any archaeological material and locations were logged by GPS. Raw-material occurrences documented across the survey programme are mapped in Supplementary Fig. 4 and provided the training data for the weights-of-evidence analysis; the 301 MSA findspots recorded across the same programme were used to validate the resulting occupation potential model.

Chronological control derives from spatial and stratigraphic correlation with the independently dated sections of ref. 16 (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). Five surveyed palaeolake localities in the eastern interior (sites 61–65) lie in the cluster of dated sections 14.3, 14.7, 15.1 and 15.3, at 6–31 km from the nearest dated section; these sections span Marine Isotope Stage 5, from about 122 ka to 67 ka and sites 61 and 62 lie within 8 km of a dated deposit. Survey localities at equivalent elevations (within ±15–20 m, accounting for Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) vertical accuracy and postdepositional deflation) and exhibiting identical lacustrine facies, such as grey marls, carbonate platforms and freshwater mollusc assemblages, are interpreted as erosionally fragmented remnants of the same palaeolake systems, correlated to the dated interval by their position on the regional piezometric gradient (Extended Data Fig. 3 and Supplementary Information, section 3).

To evaluate whether dual-resource availability predicts MP/MSA settlement, a spatial model of human occupation potential for the Arabian Peninsula was developed, integrating water proximity and lithic raw-material occurrence. Water source locations were reconstructed by combining the HydroRIVERS global drainage network64, filtered to rivers with upstream catchment areas equivalent to or more than 1,000 km2. Modelled drainage networks in areas with Quaternary aeolian geology were excluded6. Rivers were buffered by Strahler stream order to approximate channel width65.

Raw-material presence is defined by geological maps (Supplementary Information, sections 5.3 and 5.5). Here the Peninsula-wide model differs in construction from the regional Oman model (Extended Data Fig. 1). In Oman, the probability of raw-material occurrence was estimated by a weights-of-evidence analysis informed by systematic survey of raw-material occurrence. No comparable raw-material survey exists at the Peninsula scale, so the raw-material layer was derived directly from the geological map as the presence or absence of knappable lithologies in each mapped formation. Lithic raw-material suitability was assessed on the basis of conchoidal fracture properties characteristic of cryptocrystalline silicates, namely chert, quartzite, quartz, chalcedony, rhyolite and quartzitic or silicified limestone or sandstone. Because this layer is defined from geology independently of the archaeological sites, the distribution of documented MP/MSA sites provides a test of the model rather than an input to it.

Human occupation potential was classified for each resource layer independently. For both the Oman and the Peninsula-wide models, water-based potential was defined by distance thresholds corresponding to the 50th, 75th and 95th percentiles of observed site-to-water distances (high, 3; medium, 2; and low, 1 potential, respectively). In Oman, weights-of-evidence raw-material probabilities were classified into three potential classes by K-means clustering. All raw-material types were treated as equal; in the Peninsula-wide model, geological units with at least one of these raw materials were assigned a value of 1. This represents a necessary simplification of lithic resources, because knappability, nodule size, abundance and surface accessibility differ substantially between lithologies and the equal weighting is therefore a conservative limitation of the classification. These layers were combined into a single human occupation potential surface that is effectively limited to where raw materials are present and scaled by proximity to water resources (Supplementary Information, section 5). Correlation between the two resource layers is weak and slightly negative across the Oman model domain (Pearson’s r = −0.15 across the model domain), indicating that water-proximity and raw-material probability vary largely independently rather than jointly expressing a single geomorphological setting.

The dual-resource human occupation model was validated against the observed distribution of MP/MSA sites using Monte Carlo simulation. For each of 999 iterations, modelled human occupation potential values were sampled at random locations in the study area, equal in number to the known sites. A 95% confidence envelope was calculated from the ensemble of simulated distributions and compared with the observed distribution to test whether sites are preferentially associated with zones of high modelled potential. To further confirm that including raw material availability improves prediction of site locations across the Arabian Peninsula, two logistic regression models were compared. Known archaeological site locations were paired with a set of randomly generated background points (n = 10 × known site count) sampled from the study extent with a 100-m buffer around known sites to avoid pseudo-absences. Of the 363 compiled sites, 362 fall within the modelled extent and enter the comparison. Water-based potential values and raw-material availability-based potential values were independently extracted at each site and background location. A baseline model predicted archaeological site presence based on water proximity alone and a full model added raw-material availability. Model improvement was assessed by likelihood ratio test and discriminative performance of each model was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) (Extended Data Fig. 2).

The sensitivity of the resulting area of human occupation potential to raw-material classification error was assessed by a bootstrap analysis that flipped the presence or absence value of a randomly selected 5% and 10% of the geological context polygons, drawn uniformly across the mapped geology rather than targeted at units of higher classification uncertainty. The percentage of the area with water-based occupation potential retained when filtered for raw-material presence was calculated for each iteration and the observed percentage based on the raw-material availability map described above was compared with the bootstrapped values for the various label error rates (Extended Data Fig. 5).

Topographic roughness was evaluated as a potential confounding variable with raw-material availability. Elevation data from the GEDTM 120 m global model66 were reprojected to a Lambert azimuthal equal-area grid centred on the Arabian Peninsula at 104.2-m resolution and roughness was calculated as the difference between maximum and minimum elevation in a 3 × 3 cell neighbourhood (the queen neighbourhood). Cells of zero roughness accounted for 0.29% of the surface and were retained without transformation. Roughness at the 363 documented MP/MSA sites was compared with 3,630 background points drawn under the same 100-m exclusion buffer applied in the AUC analysis. Roughness on raw-material-bearing and barren geology was compared using 19,982 points sampled at random across the mapped geology, weighting each formation by its mapped area (Extended Data Fig. 4b). Nested logistic regression models were then compared by AUC to test whether roughness improved discrimination over the combined water and raw-material model. Because the AUC is a rank statistic rather than a likelihood, it can decrease when an uninformative predictor is added.

All analyses are observational and correlational; no experimental groups were allocated and no blinding or randomization applied. Monte Carlo validation and the bootstrap sensitivity analysis each used 999 iterations or resamples under a fixed random seed. Background locations for the roughness comparison were drawn at random from the modelled extent and the reported test statistics vary within approximately 0.02 of the values given across repeated draws. Statistical tests are two-sided throughout. The principal field result, freshwater present but archaeologically visible occupation absent, was recorded at all 55 palaeolake localities across the full extent of the transect. The complete R workflow and all input datasets are archived at Zenodo and OSF, with the seed set for the Monte Carlo and bootstrap procedures.

Most MP/MSA findspots used in the spatial analyses are surface occurrences lacking stratigraphic or chronometric control. Technocultural attribution relies on the presence of prepared-core technology diagnostic of the MP/MSA: Levallois reduction systems (preferential, recurrent centripetal and convergent), Nubian Levallois types 1 and 2, together with characteristic flake and point products (Levallois flakes, Levallois points and retouched points on Levallois blanks). Assemblages dominated by bifacial reduction (Lower Palaeolithic) or by blade technology on single-platform cores (Upper Palaeolithic) were excluded. Sites with mixed assemblages spanning several periods were included only where MP/MSA components were demonstrably present as discrete spatial concentrations or where diagnostic MP/MSA core technology was distinguishable from other temporal components. The same typological criteria were applied consistently to the Oman dataset (n = 301) and to the Peninsula-wide compilation (n = 363), following the technocultural attributions of the original publications. The Oman records form a subset of the Peninsula-wide compilation. The two analyses are therefore independent in their raw-material layers, the Peninsula surface being derived from 1:2,000,000 regional geology without reference to the Oman survey, rather than in their site samples. Site records in both compilations derive from published survey and excavation reports; the original publication for each locality is given in the reference field of the deposited database.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

GPS coordinates, field photographs and survey documentation from the Rub’ al Khali crossing expedition are archived in an OSF repository (https://osf.io/4mw23). The geotagged ground photographs have been deposited in the OSF repository and indexed by locality identifier, so that they can be inspected directly against the records in the Supplementary Data. We note that photography was directed at features warranting record, principally palaeolake deposits, mollusc and eggshell occurrences and raw-material exposures. Localities at which no such features were present are therefore not represented in the archive. The georeferenced MP/MSA site database for the Arabian Peninsula (n = 363), Oman survey database (n = 301 MSA findspots from 44 campaigns), raw-material occurrence records from the Oman survey programme, geological raw-material classifications and modelled surfaces of potential human occupation are archived at OSF (https://osf.io/4mw23) and available at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21758429)67. Peninsula-scale geological mapping is from the USGS digital geological map of the Arabian Peninsula; Oman geology is from the 1:250,000 Geological Map of the Sultanate of Oman; drainage networks are from HydroRIVERS; survey-locality elevations are from SRTM, and the elevation model used for terrain analysis is GEDTM; bathymetry and topography are from GEBCO; coastlines and national boundaries are from Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com). All are publicly available from their respective providers. Published OSL ages used for chronological control are reported in their original sources and compiled in Supplementary Table 4. Source data are provided with this paper.

The complete analytical workflow for spatial modelling of human occupation potential, comprising weights-of-evidence raw-material modelling, palaeodrainage proximity classification, combined model generation, Monte Carlo validation, logistic regression with AUC comparison, bootstrap sensitivity analysis and topographic roughness analysis, is provided as executable R scripts and notebooks at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21758429)67 and at OSF (https://osf.io/4mw23). The workflow is modular and transferable, and users can substitute regional geological maps and drainage networks to assess human occupation potential for stone-tool-dependent populations in any study area with published geological and hydrological data. Code is released under an MIT licence.

(a) Human occupation potential based on distance to reconstructed palaeodrainage networks (total upstream area ≥ 1,000 km2). Proximity to water classified as high (dark green), medium (green), or low (light green) probability. (b) Human occupation potential based on probability of knappable raw material occurrence, derived from 1:250,000 geological mapping of chert-bearing formations. (c) Combined dual-resource model integrating water proximity and raw material availability. High-potential zones (dark green) are restricted to areas where both resources co-occur at their highest human occupation potential, predominantly on the Dhofar Nejd plateau and western Hajar mountain piedmont. Interior regions register as low potential despite high water availability scores. Small red dots indicate MP/MSA sites. (d) Statistical validation: proportion of known MP/MSA sites (n = 301) across modelled human occupation potential, compared with the median (blue dashed line) and 2.5th to 97.5th percentile range (blue shading) of 999 simulations under a spatially random null distribution.

Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves comparing classification performance using water-based potential only (red line, AUC = 0.695) and water- and raw material availability-based potentials together (blue line, AUC = 0.768). The addition of raw material availability significantly improves predictive accuracy (two-sided DeLong’s test, P = 4.42 × 10−17). The dashed grey line represents chance-level performance (AUC = 0.50).

Blue circles show palaeolake deposits documented during the Rub’ al Khali crossing expedition (n = 55); red diamonds show Matter et al.16 sampling localities (n = 13). The dashed line indicates linear regression through survey localities (adjusted R2 = 0.913, F(1, 53) = 570.8, P = 4.8 × 10−30), with light green shading showing the 95% confidence interval of the fitted regression line. The consistent east-directed decline in elevation (~71.7 m per degree longitude) reflects the regional topographic gradient from the Arabian Shield toward the Persian Gulf. Matter et al.16 palaeolake sites show a mean absolute deviation of 30.3 m from the regression model, supporting the spatial continuity of these lacustrine systems across the central Rub’ al Khali.

(a) Empirical cumulative distribution of topographic roughness at documented MP/MSA sites (n = 363) and at background locations (n = 3,630). Sites occupy somewhat rougher terrain (median 5.44 m against 3.47 m; two-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov D = 0.307, P < 2 × 10−16), though the effect is small (Cliff’s δ = 0.197). (b) Roughness on geological formations bearing knappable lithologies (n = 8,644 points) and on formations lacking them (n = 11,338 points), sampled at random across the mapped geology so that formations are weighted by area. Knappable lithologies occur disproportionately on low-relief terrain (median 2.19 m against 4.50 m; Cliff’s δ = −0.253; two-sided Spearman ρ = −0.217, P < 2 × 10−16). The two variables are therefore inversely related, and roughness cannot generate the observed association between raw material availability and site distribution.

Violin plots show the distribution of the percentage of water-proximal area lacking raw materials across 999 bootstrap iterations at each label error rate (n = 999 per tier); box centre lines are medians, box bounds the 25th and 75th percentiles, whiskers the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range, and plotted points values beyond that range. At each iteration the presence/absence value was flipped for a randomly selected 5% or 10% of the 5,977 mapped geological polygons (298 and 597 polygons respectively), drawn uniformly across the geology rather than targeted at units of higher classification uncertainty. The red dashed horizontal line denotes the observed percentage of water-proximal areas without raw materials (56.8%). Across 999 iterations the area lacking raw material averaged 56.3% (95% interval 50.1 to 59.9%) at a 5% label error rate and 55.7% (47.9 to 61.2%) at 10%, with the observed value in both distributions.

#1341. The shifting sands of research independence: why mid-career scientists crave security

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Karen Hinxman leads the White Rose University Consortium, a strategic partnership between the universities of York, Leeds and Sheffield, UK.

Research independence can create career uncertainty.Credit: molchanovdmitry/iStock via Getty

Early-career researchers are well aware of the uncertainties that an academic career can bring. Nevertheless, many expect that if they remain in academia, their careers will progress in a relatively familiar way: after completing a doctorate, they will move into a postdoctoral position, establish research independence, obtain a permanent post and, eventually, enter a more settled stage of academic life.

The conversations that my colleagues and I have had with established researchers while working on the White Rose Established Researchers project — a collaboration between the UK universities of Leeds, Sheffield and York that aims to support career development — suggest that career progression is often much less linear.

Research independence, which is characterized as a researcher’s ability to lead and sustain an original programme of research, is typically associated with the mid-career stage in academia. It brings with it a fresh set of challenges: how to sustain research while leading people, managing competing responsibilities and prioritizing the tasks that can have the greatest impact. The researchers whom we interviewed rarely spoke about having ‘made it’; instead, they described having to regularly refresh and revise how they think about their careers, in circumstances of increasing uncertainty.

It is striking how little attention has been paid to understanding the period between establishing research independence and the later stages of an academic career. Universities have invested heavily in supporting early-career researchers and have developed sophisticated programmes for senior leaders. Yet, relatively little attention has been given to the distinctive experiences of academics occupying the space between those career stages.

Our collaboration explored how established researchers experience the middle stage of their career. Across four months, we interviewed 27 established researchers, held two focus groups with them, sent them a follow-up survey to validate our findings and mapped institutional resources across the three universities.

Because no widely accepted definition of an established researcher exists, we defined them as “an academic who has achieved functional independence and institutional recognition in their research capacity, whilst continuing to develop their professional identity and navigate complex career transitions”.

The established-researcher career stage is characterized by a distinct research agenda, the capacity to secure and manage funding, a strong track record of scholarly outputs, recognition in relevant research communities and the ability to make substantive intellectual contributions to their field.

Across disciplines, established researchers described a shared experience of juggling various, often competing, responsibilities that span research, teaching, leadership, administration and collaboration. The challenge was rarely any individual role; instead, it was the continual negotiation of priorities across them.

As we analysed the interviews, we found that researchers were making sense of this complexity in different ways. To help to illuminate these recurring patterns, we outlined four personas that can be used to articulate different approaches to navigating the established stage of an academic career.

No researcher fits perfectly into a single persona. Many recognized aspects of themselves in more than one and described moving between them over time. But we developed these personas to understand how researchers think about success, make decisions and respond to the continuing complexity of academic life.

For some established researchers, academic life revolves around people as much as projects. Alongside developing their own research programmes, they recruit and train staff, secure funding and create opportunities for others. Many described an important transition from being the person who mainly conducts research to becoming the one who galvanizes the collective efforts of a team to enable research to happen.

Career planning strategies for scientists

Career planning strategies for scientists

For anyone hoping to lead a research group, this persona offers an important reminder: independence entails leadership, delegation, shaping research culture and balancing investment in others with maintenance of your own scientific expertise. Many researchers described the challenge of redefining success as their role shifted from doing research themselves to enabling the work of others. What got them to this point in their career was not always what was required to succeed in the next stage. This work is not routinely celebrated, yet it is fundamental to the long-term success of many research environments.

Many early-career researchers assume that becoming established means leading ever-larger groups. However, independent scholars organize their careers around sustained intellectual contribution: their influence comes from the ideas they develop and the scholarship they produce, pushing forwards thinking in their discipline. They might collaborate widely, but their work is characterized less by organizational expansion than by continuity of intellectual purpose.

One of their greatest challenges is protecting the quality thinking time that sustained scholarship requires while juggling the pressures of increasingly fragmented academic roles. Many also described the challenge of gaining recognition for forms of contribution that do not depend on large-scale grant funding, including editorial work, intellectual leadership and the development of scholarly communities that stimulate fresh debates and directions for research.

Some established researchers described careers centred on leading collaborative research on a large scale. Whether coordinating multidisciplinary teams, cross-institutional partnerships or large funded programmes, they bring together people, expertise and opportunities across several projects that do not necessarily form a single coherent research programme. Rather than building one permanent team, these researchers create successive collaborations that evolve as ideas, funding opportunities and partnerships emerge.

Their biggest challenge is maintaining a coherent sense of purpose while managing numerous projects, partnerships and opportunities simultaneously. As their portfolio grows, deciding which opportunities to pursue and which to decline becomes an increasingly important part of their professional development.

#1340. Slow and dull Man Utd are just not good enough

Manchester United are like John Toshack’s duvet. You fix one problem – being far too vulnerable to conceding goals – only to create another – lacking the threat to score. It is all very Meh United not Man United. The indisputable fact is they are just not very entertaining to watch. They are slow and dull.

In the end it also points to another thing. The thing highlighted in midweek by Lisandro Martínez after the Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid: they do not have the strength in depth to compete.

What they do have appears to not be fit for purpose. Certainly Michael Carrick, the under-pressure manager, is struggling to get the best out of the resources he has.

“It’s like a duvet,” Toshack, the former Real Madrid and Wales manager, famously said of football. “If you pull it up, your feet get cold. If you pull it down, your shoulders get cold.”

There will have been times in the last few days, with the intense criticism and scrutiny over his future, when Carrick will have simply felt like dragging that duvet up over his head and keeping it there.

Defeat by Leeds United would have been unthinkable. It would have put Carrick under potentially intolerable pressure in what appears to be a pivotal week, with Como away in the Champions League and a home Premier League fixture against Bournemouth in the coming days.

Was this a lifeline or the tightening of the noose for Carrick? Time will soon tell. The relief of avoiding defeat was tempered by the reality of it now being just one win in their opening seven league games – at home to newly promoted Ipswich Town – and they are down in 13th place. It is six games without a win in all competitions.

That is unacceptable and is their fewest number of league victories in a top-flight campaign since 1986-87. Back then they sacked their manager in November and brought in a certain Alex Ferguson.

The hard truth is Carrick needs to start collecting some “Ws” in those results columns. United are already 14 points behind leaders Manchester City and five outside the probable Champions League places. Qualifying again for that tournament must be the minimum expectation.

Ruben Amorim, Carrick’s predecessor, lost his job within 24 hours of the same 1-1 scoreline at Elland Road last season – dismissed after Martínez-like explosive comments again aimed at director of football Jason Wilcox. Carrick will not suffer the same fate after this, but the ice is becoming increasingly thin.

We have seen this movie before at United. A slow start to the season, a period of drift, falling out of contention, no reaction on the pitch, backing from the hierarchy that becomes increasingly unconvincing. And then a change.

Can Carrick, who genuinely does still retain support at the highest level, alter that pattern? Does he have it in him? Is he too passive like his team? Carrick said this draw felt like a “fresh start”, but on this evidence that comment can be classified as wildly optimistic.

Having directed his criticism at the United hierarchy, and specifically Wilcox, the former Leeds winger who was here, over a lack of summer signings, Martínez apologised and was named in the starting XI. But the Argentine only lasted to half-time, withdrawn injured with a tight thigh, and sat watching the second half with his hood up over his head.

What United did sign in the last window was three midfielders – at a cost of £155m – and all three started: Carlos Baleba alongside Andrey Santos with Youri Tielemans in the No 10 role, which meant Bruno Fernandes was pushed out to the left, from where he constantly wanted to come in-field, with Amad Diallo on the right.

Carrick talked of having a “fresh spine” as well as that fresh start. But it did not make for a potent combination even if, further forward, Bryan Mbeumo played through the middle and scored one. He should have scored another.

Bryan Mbeumo finds the net this time to put Manchester United 1-0 up at Leeds! 🔴 https://t.co/NKDIhlUND1

But beyond that United created little. “It was a dominant performance against Man United,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds manager, claimed. He was right. If one team deserved to win it was his. They had the chances but snatched at them with Anton Stach, in injury time, having a weak shot cleared off the line by Martínez’s replacement Noussair Mazraoui after a mistake by goalkeeper Senne Lammens. Stach had to score.

United were ahead at half-time. Mbeumo had headed wastefully wide when unmarked but did well to force his way past James Justin and meet a low cross from Tielemans to poke the ball home. The way the usually undemonstrative Carrick punched the air in his technical area showed the pressure he felt. It was something to build on. To gain control.

Leeds had started well but did not really pose much of a threat – beyond forcing Lammens to save well from Nico Elvedi’s downward header – and maybe the earlier kick-off subdued the crowd. This was far from a bear pit.

But after the break, Leeds were comfortably the better side. The nature of their equalising goal, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin too strong and alert for first Baleba and then Mbeumo to fire in from a corner, exposed the enduring softness at the heart of United.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalises for Leeds against Manchester United 👊 https://t.co/mnpyxZJKbm

And that must be addressed by Carrick, especially as he appeared to sacrifice attacking intent by shoring up defensively. But that duvet is looking far too inadequate right now. Or Carrick is making it appear so.

Michael Carrick says he has put on “the headphones” this week in an effort to drown out the noise, but admitted Manchester United have to stop their struggles from snowballing.

United sit just two points above the relegation zone after a 1-1 draw at Leeds left them with just one win from their opening seven Premier League matches.

Carrick claimed the result felt like a “fresh start” after a week in which Lisandro Martínez publicly apologised for criticising Jason Wilcox, the United director of football, and the Old Trafford board.

But the United manager acknowledged their position “doesn’t look too good” and that they must start winning soon to stop the club from entering another doom cycle.

“Listen, we’re not accepting it as everything’s great by any stretch, so I’m realistic with that,” said the United manager, who claimed “the headphones have been on this week”.

“But sometimes you do struggle, sometimes there’s a bit of it where you have to find a way through it. We haven’t really had to go through that yet [before now] and we have to find a way through it.

“There has been a cycle at times here over a period of time when it can go in different directions. We’ve got to be stable enough to keep doing the right things for the right reasons as a group, and we’re more than capable of winning football matches.

“I understand the situation doesn’t look too good if you look at it from a certain way, but I’ve no doubts we can go on a good run.”

United face Como in the Champions League in Italy on Wednesday before Bournemouth visit Old Trafford four days later.

Carrick said he remains convinced United can still have a strong campaign, despite their worst start to a season for 40 years. I know what we’ve got in the changing room, where we want to get to, how we want to get there,” he said. “We know we can do it.

“We’ve done it for some time, and we feel we’re a better group now, and I do feel that. Sometimes it doesn’t always show, but you get a feeling and I’m encouraged by a lot of things. And if we keep doing the right things, I think we can still have a really good season.”

Asked if he would be putting the headphones back on this week ahead of two more pivotal games, Carrick added: “Nah, it’s always quiet for me.”

Martínez was substituted at half-time at Elland Road with a tight thigh just days after his tirade at club executives and Marcus Rashford was left out for “purely tactical” reasons. “Nothing personal, the front players were doing a good job on and off the ball,” Carrick said. “Everyone is ready for Wednesday.”

The Leeds boss told Sky Sports: “We are slightly disappointed it is just a point. Overall, I felt it was not necessary to be losing at half time but it is still Manchester United. Second half, we got the equaliser, we should have kept up the dominance, too many strikes went over the crossbar but it was overall a solid performance. We should have won the game but we move on.

“We took it as a compliment that we have done many things right over the last month if we were seen as favourites against Manchester Untiedbut we have earned this. We wanted to prove the comments right.

“We were the dominant side but we couldn’t capitalise as we lacked quality in and around the box.

“It says a lot about how much respect we have earned. Overall, this is where we are at the moment and overall, it is a good place to be.

“It is still difficult in this league to win points. You have to be clinical and be very, very effective but we have to keep going.”

Speaking to Sky Sports, he said: “I think we could’ve played with a bit more quality in the final third, particularly in the first half. We were getting good quality in the box but just not enough numbers.

“We made sure in the second half we came out with more confidence going forward. I think we were unlucky not to win the game.

“They tried to [match us up formation-wise]. Not surprised given what happened last season. They were probably looking at our physical output and the way we liked to play and tried to go man-for-man.

“It took us a little bit to adjust to it, but I don’t think it was too difficult to adjust. It was more down to us and maybe a lack of quality in the final third.”

Brighton & Hove Albion 5 Crystal Palace 0

It’s all over at Elland Road, with Leeds and Man Utd playing out a competitive draw. Mbeumo’s opener was cancelled out by Calvert-Lewin’s equaliser in a game that was low on attacking quality and chances. Ultimately, a draw was a very fair reflection of the match. Man Utd are 14th and winless in six games across all competitions, while Leeds move into the top seven.

FULL-TIME: Dominic Calvert-Lewin earns a point for Leeds against Manchester United 💪 https://t.co/yDzLRE3Ir5

There are two yellow cards in quick succession as Ampadu is cautioned for a late tackle on Amad. Andrey Santos runs over and barges into the Leeds captain to earn himself a booking. The referee quickly calms then drama down.

Unconvincing goalkeeping from Lammens as he only punches Ampadu’s cross as far as Stach, whose tame shot squeezes through the Belgian’s legs. However, it’s blocked by the Man Utd defence and Lammens eventually gathers the ball.

There will be four minutes of added time. Can either side snatch a late victory?

Three times now United have looked like they’re about to get away down the flanks in the last few minutes and each time they’ve been flagged offside (Amad twice, Mbeumo once) and each occasion the player was able to look across the line. Carrick looked to the heavens. And he’s right to be frustrated. So avoidable.

Nmecha and Maguire challenge for the ball in the air, with the Man Utd defender bumping into the back of the Leeds substitute’s head. The crowd half-heartedly appeal for a penalty, but it’s quickly checked and cleared by VAR.

Carrick responds with a positive, attacking switch as Tielemans departs for Cunha.

Farke makes another change for Leeds as Longstaff replaces Tanaka in midfield.

Excellently goalkeeping from Trafford, who dashes out of his six-yard box to collect Andrey Santos’ pass and keep the ball in his grasp while staying in his box under the watchful eye of Mbeumo.

Dalot drives forward and leads a counter-attack. He passes to Amad, who forces a corner as Leeds get back well and recover. Man Utd take a clever short corner routine, but it ends with Mount scuffing an effort wide.

Both teams make changes. For Leeds, Nmecha replaces Okafor, while Mount enters the action for Man Utd as Baleba is withdrawn. The Englishman will sit alongside Andrey Santos in the away side’s midfield pivot.

From presentable range, Fernandes curls an effort straight into Trafford’s arms. Dalot then fails to adequately deal with a cross, heading the ball only as far as Stach. However, the Leeds midfielder wildly lashes his strike over the bar.

United were under that cosh in that period after Leeds equalised but they’ve gained a foothold back in the game now and a bit of frustration has crept in among the home fans. Stach the third player to fire high over the bar. Could go either way this.

How much longer will Carrick wait before making some changes in forward areas? His side need some renewed attacking impetus. The Man Utd head coach has Rashford, Cunha, Mount and Zirkzee all on the bench to choose from.

Okafor attempts to spearhead a Leeds break by playing in Calvert-Lewin. However, his pass is poor and it’s intercepted by Maguire. Amad is down after being caught by Tanaka earlier in that phase of play.

On the turn, Fernandes drags a low effort wide of the far post in a rare attacking flurry for Man Utd in this second half.

Ampadu feels Leeds should have a penalty as he collides with Maguire at a corner. The Man Utd defender hauls the Leeds captain to the floor. It’s been checked and cleared by VAR, but Maguire was taking a huge risk there.

Michael Carrick will surely be angry at the way Manchester United have started the second-half. One-nil up they have been far too slow and casual - highlighted by Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s goal which was embarrassingly easy to score from a corner. Leeds now on top and a huge few minutes ahead for Carrick.

Gudmundsson’s searching cross can’t quite find Calvert-Lewin as Man Utd scramble it clear. The away side’s backline has three defenders playing out of position, and they’ve been made to pay by Leeds’ leveller.

How will Man Utd cope with that setback? Leeds are putting them under serious pressure and have flown out of the blocks since the break as Tanaka volleys over from outside the penalty area.

The hosts finally have something to shout about at Elland Road! Leeds have a corner and Muharemovic beats Mazraoui to the delivery. The defender glances the ball to Calvert-Lewin, who holds off Mbeumo before smashing a close-range half-volley into the bottom corner. Elland Road goes wild and Leeds now have the momentum at the start of this second half.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalises for Leeds against Manchester United 👊 https://t.co/mnpyxZJKbm

It looks like a straight swap as Mazraoui slots in as a centre back, with Yoro continuing to deputise on the right.

We are back under way the second half. Martinez has been withdrawn at half-time, with Mazraoui on as his replacement, while Leeds are unchanged.

That is a really good half for Manchester United. More for the scoreline than the performance, although they have grown into the game after a sluggish start. Bryan Mbeumo’s goal will come as a huge relief to Michael Carrick. Leeds, in truth, have been a disappointment although they were denied the opening goal by Senne Lammens with a fine save. They needs to raise the tempo and the crowd. It is far too quiet. If Manchester United can hold on or build on this it will be a huge result for their under-pressure manager.

Carrick will be delighted with that first half. Man Utd have frustrated Leeds, defended valiantly and found the all-important breakthrough thanks to Mbeumo’s opener. Despite all the drama leading up to this game, Man Utd look really organised and unified, limiting Leeds to very little in forward areas.

Ahead at the break 👊🔴 https://t.co/rSSC8Pu4iG

There will be two minutes of added time. Can Man Utd protect their lead until the break?

Bogle drives into Man Utd’s box and squeezes a shot through a sea of bodies. However, it trickles into Lammens’ arms.

A big few minutes here for Manchester United. They need to see this half out. The goal has really steadied them but important they take that lead into the interval.

Calvert-Lewin attempts to latch onto Bogle’s clipped cross, but he directs it harmlessly wide.

Carrick’s game plan has worked perfectly so far. Man Utd soaked up the early pressure with their determined defending, before growing in confidence over the last 10 minutes. Mbeumo’s goal was much deserved.

You could see what that goal meant to Michael Carrick. He’s not one to show his emotions but he punches the air and wears the steely look of a man who knows how important it was to get the first goal here.

Mbeumo missed an earlier chance, but he makes no mistake with that one! Amad slips in Tielemans, who whips a magnificent cross into Mbeumo. The forward shows great composure and guides the delivery into the bottom corner.

Bryan Mbeumo finds the net this time to put Manchester United 1-0 up at Leeds! 🔴 https://t.co/NKDIhlUND1

The crowd loves that as Trafford sprints way out of his box almost to the halfway line to beat Amad to a ball over the top. Man Utd then make a promising break through Mbeumo, whose tame effort is easily gathered by Trafford.

Bogle attempts to take everyone on as he dribbles into Man Utd’s penalty area. He glides away from Dalot and Martinez, but overruns it, allowing Maguire to come across and shepherd the ball out of play.

Chants of “you soft southern b------” from the Leeds fans every time a Manchester United player goes down injured. Just a reminder that Leeds is actually only 22 miles further north than Manchester.

The away side are growing into this contest, with a slick move seeing Baleba find Dalot. The right back sprints into Leeds’ box, but he’s tackled well by Bogle.

Mbeumo misses a massive opportunity! Tielemans clips in a cross and an unmarked Mbeumo finds space between Elvedi and Muharemovic but heads wide. He has to get that on target.

Bryan Mbeumo comes close to giving Manchester United the lead 😬 https://t.co/j5PFXa2Uhe

Leeds test Lammens! Stach whips in a free kick, which is met by Elvedi, whose downward header is parried away by Lammens. That’s Leeds’ best chance so far, but the Man Utd goalkeeper did his job.

Leeds have enjoyed nearly 70% possession, but they’re yet to have a shot of any note. That’s testament to Man Utd’s competitiveness and organisation. Bogle then digs out a promising cross, but Yoro heads it away at the back post.

In fairness to Man Utd, they’re defending solidly and doing well to frustrate Leeds. Gudmundsson is then carded for catching Andrey Santos on his ankle with a very unpleasant challenge. It’s been such a physical and scruffy match so far.

Risky from Fernandes as he lunges in with a dangerous challenge on Muharemovic. Leeds then break as Martinez misses his tackle on Calvert-Lewin, but Stach’s cross is blocked. When the ball eventually goes out of play, Fernandes is booked for that earlier challenge. He can have no complaints.

United staff aggrieved that Fernandes should be booked but Ampadu escape a yellow card before then for arguably a worse challenge on Mbeumo, whom he caught thick on the ankle with his studs.

🫡 Ethan Ampadu starts as captain for the 100th time, becoming the youngest player to reach that milestone since Billy Bremner! https://t.co/80YrU08S3s

No early rhythm in this game so far. It’s still a little frantic at the moment, with Leeds having most of the ball and trying to force the issue.

Leeds crunch into a couple of heavy challenges on the Man Utd players in these early exchanges. Stach is eventually penalised for a strong tackle, but it’s a purposeful start from the hosts.

Interestingly, it looks like Fernandes is starting centrally in the ‘false nine’ position, with Mbeumo and Amad out on the wings. The Man Utd captain started out wide in Spain on Wednesday - an experiment that definitely did not work.

We are under way at Elland. Can Leeds pile more misery on Man Utd or will the visitors answer their critics with a much-needed win?

Leeds striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin was the only player not to take the knee prior to kick-off for the Premier League’s ‘No Room for Racism’ campaign. The gesture from the other players was roundly booed by a lot of the fans inside Elland Road.

Both teams are out on the pitch, with kick-off fast approaching.

With just 10 minutes until kick-off, here’s a recap of the two squads.

Leeds: Trafford, Justin, Elvedi, Muharemovic, Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson, Stach, Okafor, Calvert-Lewin.
