Man Utd: Lammens, Yoro, Maguire, Martinez, Dalot, Santos, Baleba, Fernandes, Tielemans, Diallo, Mbeumo.

Subs: Darlow, Mazraoui, de Ligt, Mount, Rashford, Cunha, Zirkzee, Lacey, Amass.

"I'm torn a little bit" Gary Neville says there should be some 'consequences' for Lisandro Martínez's comments after Man Utd's loss to Atlético Madrid ⤵️ https://t.co/oz8Mj24NuH

"We've moved on" Michael Carrick on Lisandro Martínez starting for Man Utd 🔴 https://t.co/mKVnI3gTrT

"We know what we need to do today" Ethan Ampadu speaks ahead of Leeds' clash with Man Utd ⚔️ https://t.co/wT5H5uzX7b

There have been wide open spaces in Manchester United’s side for opponents to exploit this season so it’s no surprise to see Michael Carrick keep faith with an extra body in midfield. It could make for a rather disjointed set up.

Lisandro Martinez keeps his place despite his rant at the Old Trafford board in midweek but the bigger concern has been his individual performances this season - they have been nowhere near good enough and he’s brought extra scrutiny on himself with the tirade. Bruno Fernandes is going to have to operate out wide you would think if Youri Tielemans plays centrally ahead of Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos.

Leeds are the kind of compact, organised, aggressive in-your-face team United have tended to struggle against in recent years. They were good in defeat to Arsenal last weekend and showcased their considerable threat in the 4-1 win over Newcastle. Expect a white-hot atmosphere at Elland Road. They cannot stand Manchester United in these parts.

Lisandro Martínez delivered a strong and powerful message to his Manchester United team-mates: if you’re playing terribly, use the director of football as a punchbag and you might become a hero.

It is a popular play in a world in which certain players have become as adept at scapegoat-hunting as man-marking. Passionately speak about what someone else at your football club is doing wrong – particularly the unloved executives – and cast yourself as a whistleblower, selflessly exposing the truth that the long-suffering supporters deserve.

Such internal fights make for great drama, unless your own club is caught in the middle of it.

That’s why in the immediate aftermath of Martínez’s scathing comments about Jason Wilcox following the Champions League defeat by Atlético Madrid, there was a division between those who celebrated the Argentine speaking out and those who felt it was self-serving, a convenient deflection by an out-of-form player in the final year of his contract.

The narrative is completely dominated by the drama around Man Utd, which should suit Leeds perfectly. All eyes and pressure is on their opponents, and they have every reason to feel confident ahead of this huge clash at Elland Road.

"You can't be the biggest spenders every season when you're not being successful" @Carra23 discusses the criticism of Manchester United's spending 💰 https://t.co/6GKfgozPXW

There’s a lot to unpack with this Man Utd team. Lisandro Martinez starting grabs the headlines, while Carlos Baleba begins his first Premier League match for his new club. Luke Shaw remains unavailable through injury, with Leny Yoro, who was sent off in midweek, deputising at full-back. Kobbie Mainoo is also sidelined, while Matheus Cunha and Marcus Rashford are benched. With Benjamin Sesko still out, Bryan Mbeumo starts up top and is likely to be supported out wide by Amad Diallo and Bruno Fernandes.

The big news is that Lisandro Martinez starts for the visitors, despite his scathing outburst earlier in the week. Michael Carrick also starts Carlos Baleba for the second match running, and he’s partnered in midfield by Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans. Captain Bruno Fernandes could begin out wide again, just as he did against Atletico Madrid, with Bryan Mbeumo likely to lead the line up top.

It's time for team news! ⏰ 🔴 Here's your United starting XI... 🤳 @Snapdragon https://t.co/A5phvW4gvF

The hosts are unchanged from the side that lost to Arsenal last weekend.

📋 United XI to face Man Utd... https://t.co/SXwWXll8OS

"My focus is driving the club forward" Michael Carrick confident Man Utd can turn around their form. 🔴 https://t.co/5NZSkUpS7B

Just 10 months on from Ruben Amorim’s final game in charge of Manchester United, the club return to Elland Road on Sunday afternoon with another manager under pressure and the director of football again in the spotlight.

The difference is Michael Carrick still has a chance to determine the course of his United future whereas Amorim had already sealed his fate after a furious bust-up with Jason Wilcox 48 hours before his last game ended in a 1-1 draw with Leeds and post-match fireworks.

But even for a club never far from a crisis, it seems remarkable to think they are back in a tailspin so soon after Amorim’s sacking in early January.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League fixture between Manchester United and Leeds United at Elland Road.

Quiet week in the world of Man Utd? Don’t be silly. Following a 2-0 defeat in the Champions League against Atlético Madrid in Spain on Wednesday, defender Lisandro Martinez launched an extraordinary attack on Man Utd’s director of football Jason Wilcox and the club’s hierarchy because of a dreadful start to the campaign, which has yielded two victories in nine games across all competitions.

The Argentine criticised Man Utd’s recruitment and said he expected more, but didn’t suggest Carrick was to blame. Martinez has since apologised for his outburst and met with Wilcox, Man Utd chief executive Omar Berrada and Michael Carrick, with Telegraph Sport understanding that he’s free to play today, although his role remains unclear as we all eagerly await the team news.

Carrick is under immense pressure to get a result here in Yorkshire, with last weekend’s 1-1 draw with 10-man Tottenham at Old Trafford condemning Man Utd to their worst league start for 40 years.

With all eyes on the visitors, Leeds will be licking their lips at the prospect of piling further misery on their beleaguered opponents. Daniel Farke’s side suffered their first Premier League loss last weekend, falling 2-1 to Arsenal at the Emirates after going a goal up, but the mood remains positive after a solid start to the campaign.

Leeds are eighth and the club will be harbouring ambitions of a top-half finish in the Premier League for the first time since the 2019/20 season, with the prospect of qualifying for European football not out of the realm of possibility.

Unlike Man Utd, Leeds have a settled, reliable system that clearly suits their current squad. Elland Road will also be a cauldron of hostility and noise, given the fierce backdrop between these two bitter rivals.

This has all the ingredients to be a thrilling and fascinating watch as we bring you the latest updates, information and drama. Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news coming shortly.

#1338. Where have all the saucers flown?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Jeff Hecht is based in the Boston area where he writes factual articles about science and technology to make a living and science-fiction stories to stimulate the imagination, many of them for Nature Futures.

Holding her lunch box, Lili scanned the noon break area at the Exotic Destinations travel show. The middle-aged travel agents chattering among themselves ignored her, but a tall Black woman with snow-white hair waved.

Recognizing her from the session on tourism on the Extraterrestrial Highway, Lili walked over to ask, “May I join you?”

“Certainly,” the woman said. “My name’s Bettye, with an e at the end. I noticed you at the Extraterrestrial Highway session.”

“I’m Lili, with two l’s, two i’s and no y at all, and I saw you there. What did you think of their space alien experience?” She sat down to unpack her lunch.

“It’s changed tremendously since I was young,” Bettye said. “My parents just hoped to see a flying saucer on a long trip across the southwestern desert. Now they have cheesy roadside attractions with animated space aliens waving outside the door.”

Intrigued, Lili asked “What was it like back then?”

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

“Flying saucers were a mystery in the sixties; everybody wanted to see one. Papa was an Air Force mechanic, and pilots told him they had seen saucers. The Byrds sung about hitching a ride on a saucer. Papa always looked for saucers.”

“Do your stories help sell tours?” Lili asked.

“I wish I had travel stories, but my parents were too poor to take vacations after they immigrated from Hong Kong.”

Bettye grinned. “Oh, we loved telling those stories about looking for flying saucers, but we had to be careful we didn’t scare anyone.”

Bettye sipped her iced tea and sat back. “I saw my first saucer when we were driving through the desert. Papa drove at night because our old station wagon didn’t have air conditioning. The Moon was bright so we could see the foothills and the cacti. I fell asleep, but woke when Papa stopped. He and Mama whispered and pointed at a moonlit saucer parked a little ways away. A hatch opened and two aliens got out and walked towards us. Mama said we better go, but the car wouldn’t start. The aliens wore pale green suits and carried metal boxes that looked like old telephones. I waved, and they waved back.”

“A little,” Bettye said. “Then the boxes started talking English voices like we heard on the radio. Mama hushed me when I giggled.”

“They asked us to fly them over the mountains and tell them about the scenery. Papa laughed and said our car couldn’t fly. They said theirs could, and Mama got them to pay us to guide them. Mama was scared because she had never flown, but Papa and I had a great flight. After we landed, the aliens asked if we would guide other aliens on trips.”

“Oh yes. Papa took me along and we had a great time guiding the alien tours. They were very friendly and what they paid let me go to college.”

“That was a very successful business,” Lili said. “How long did it last?”

Bettye nodded. “Several years, until a saucer flew too close to an Air Force base. A pilot at the base jumped into a fighter and flew towards us. Papa told the aliens to fly away because the fighter might shoot us down, but their speaking boxes said ‘no civilized beings would do that’.”

“The fighter shot a missile at us. Then one alien pointed something at the missile and it vanished. The other alien pointed a box at the plane and made it move with what he called a force field. He made it land on the road. The pilot opened the door and ran away while we watched the alien melt the plane.”

The German youngster is regarded as one of the most promising goalkeeping talents in his country, and his performances have attracted attention from several leading European clubs.

Manchester United are particularly interested in his potential as they look to strengthen their long-term goalkeeping department. Seimen has impressed with his reflexes, ability to handle one-on-one situations, and composure when distributing the ball from the back.

His command of the penalty area and ability to deal with aerial threats are other qualities that make him an attractive prospect. The goalkeeper’s technical ability could make him a suitable option for United as they look to build a squad capable of competing at the highest level.

Inter Milan and Atletico Madrid are also monitoring the Stuttgart academy graduate, increasing the competition for his signature.

However, none of the interested clubs have opened formal negotiations with Stuttgart, with their current activity limited to scouting and assessing his development.

However, convincing Stuttgart to sanction his departure will not be straightforward. The Bundesliga club consider Seimen an important part of their long-term plans and hope he will eventually become their first-choice goalkeeper.

He remains under contract until June 2029, placing Stuttgart in a strong negotiating position.

According to the report, the German club could demand between €25 million and €30 million to consider selling their young goalkeeper, despite his current market value being estimated at approximately €10 million.

A January transfer is considered unlikely, with Stuttgart keen to continue his development rather than lose him prematurely.

Manchester United could therefore face a difficult battle if they decide to formalise their interest, although Seimen’s potential makes him an exciting long-term target.

#1335. Why Juventus had to register Ekhator and not Zhegrova in UEFA squad list changes

Juventus have added Jeff Ekhator to their UEFA squad list in place of injured captain Manuel Locatelli, and the competition’s registration rules decided it ahead of Edon Zhegrova.

According to TuttoMercatoWeb, the Bianconeri have finally replaced Locatelli, who had knee surgery on his meniscus in September and isn’t expected back until next year. Ekhator returned to the squad for Sunday’s 2-0 win over Napoli after a long injury lay-off.

On form, Zhegrova would have been the obvious choice. The winger has looked sharper in recent weeks and is one of Luciano Spalletti’s few fit attacking options, but he isn’t eligible.

UEFA requires every 25-man A list to include a minimum number of locally trained players: four trained at the club itself and up to four trained at other clubs in the same country.

Locatelli, who came through the youth system at Milan, counts as one of Juve’s association-trained players. That means he can only be swapped for a player in the same category.

Ekhator, a product of Genoa’s academy, fits that requirement. Zhegrova had never played in Italy before joining Juventus, so he would have taken one of the 17 unrestricted places, and those are already full.

#1331. Allegri: ‘Napoli’s Champions League fate is in our hands, but the league is more important’

Massimiliano Allegri insists Napoli’s Champions League fate is still in their own hands, but warned that turning their league form around matters more.

With quotes via TuttoMercatoWeb, the Napoli coach spoke at the Estádio do Dragão on Tuesday, before Wednesday’s game against Porto, which kicks off at 21:00 CET [20:00 GMT].

Allegri is back in the dugout after a two-match Serie A ban. During it, Napoli won 4-1 at Monza and lost 2-0 at Juventus, leaving them 10th on 14 points. In Europe, they have three points from three games after defeats in their first two matches and a 4-3 win over Bodø/Glimt.

He opened by paying tribute to Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel, who died at 30 after a collision with Andorra goalkeeper Owono during a match in Spain. “First of all, I’d like to offer my condolences to the family of Jesús de Miguel for this tragic accident to a young man, before a footballer, who lost his life,” he said.

“Tomorrow’s game is difficult, because Porto have won 10 in a row in the league, and they’ve played some good games in the Champions League too. As for us, talking is of little use, we need to put in a good performance. In the Champions League, our destiny is in our hands, because with 10 points we’d reach the play-offs at least. But then there’s the league to sort out, and that’s the most important thing.”

“Tomorrow isn’t the last chance. With 10 points you go to the play-offs. Tomorrow is an important game. Manchester is an important game but almost impossible. We’ll fight for qualification against Club Brugge, Viking and Sabah,” Allegri said.

He denied the injury crisis takes any pressure off. “It doesn’t take any pressure off, because it’s an important Champions League game against a strong team. Right now there’s no need to talk and explain. There’s only the need to act, to work, to get the injured players back and turn this negative period into a positive one.”

On Rasmus Højlund and Kevin De Bruyne, he said: “Højlund’s fever has gone. De Bruyne will train today, and afterwards we’ll see if he’s available for tomorrow.”

Asked about fears of a repeat of the season Napoli finished 10th, Allegri said: “Right now it’s time to act, not to talk. It’s not an easy moment. We’ve had mixed results and haven’t yet managed to win two league games in a row. But what’s certain is that we have to keep working, get back all the players who will return after the international break, and try to turn things around in the league, where there will be time and space to recover. In the meantime, we’re thinking about tomorrow, there’s a game to play.”

He returned Francesco Farioli’s praise. “I think Farioli, a young coach, has already achieved good results, both in the Netherlands and in Portugal. He has a very important career ahead of him.”

On the threat Porto pose at home: “We know Porto are very aggressive at home, and they have technical, physical and high-quality players. When we have the ball we’ll need to be good technically, and when we don’t we’ll need to defend well, which is something we’ve done less this season.”

Asked whether Porto would press with fewer players or match Napoli’s numbers, he said: “I don’t know, it depends on what Farioli decides. Whether it’s numbers even or an extra man, you have to behave in two completely different ways.”

#1329. Politano: ‘Napoli are fragile at the moment, but no alibi against Porto’

Matteo Politano admits Napoli are ‘fragile’ defensively and concede too easily, but mustn’t ‘use injuries as an alibi’ for the Champions League trip to FC Porto.

It kicks off at the Estadio do Dragao on Wednesday at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CET).

The Partenopei are playing catch-up in the tournament after one win and two defeats, but that is still better than their opponents, who lost all three matches so far in the Champions League.

Max Allegri’s side also stumbled in Serie A at the weekend, losing 2-0 away to Juventus.

“A difficult game awaits us tomorrow. It’s true that we have some injuries, but this mustn’t be used as an alibi, we don’t want alibis at this moment,” said Politano in his press conference.

“We are the only ones who can drag ourselves out of this situation. We’ve got to give our all on the pitch, because this is a fundamental match for us.”

The recurring problem for Napoli this season is how many goals they are conceding, and assistant manager Marco Landucci confirmed players backing off when defending is not something suggested by the coaching staff.

“When we concede goals, it’s everyone’s fault and not just the defenders, this is a team sport,” confessed Politano.

“We are fragile at the moment, we can’t seem to defend as well as we did in previous years. We lack determination in pressing the opponents, so naturally against quality players you are going to pay for that.

“We’ve got to come together as a unit and try from tomorrow to be more solid. We haven’t tested the line-up yet, so we don’t know if it’ll be three or four at the back, but it is no problem for me.”

Napoli fumbled a lead for the 3-1 Champions League defeat to Villarreal, and Politano made a very costly error with a howler of a back-pass.

“Unfortunately, we can do nothing about the past, we need to focus on the future,” added the winger.

“I challenge myself every single day to give more, I’ve won a lot with this team, but I’ve got to keep pushing. It’s not an easy situation, we’ve all got to come together and stay concentrated at all times.

“Porto are a strong side, they attack in numbers and know how to keep the ball for long spells, so there are moments when we’ll be pinned back, waiting to then launch forward on the counter.

“It is fortunate that we have the opportunity so soon after the Juventus match to prove ourselves all over again, we were lacking something that we need to show tomorrow.”

Nicholas E. Banovich is in the Bioinnovation and Genome Sciences Division, Translational Genomics Research Institute (TGen), Phoenix, Arizona 85004, USA.

Four years ago, scientists reported findings from the OneK1K project1. This large-scale initiative involved sequencing RNA from cells donated by around 1,000 people with the goal of identifying genetic variants that affect gene expression and disease risk. An expansion of that project, TenK10K, now combines single-cell RNA-sequencing data with other kinds of molecular profiling with the aim of mapping and characterizing genetic variants in 50 million cells from a diverse cohort of 10,000 individuals. Writing in Nature, Cuomo et al.2, Xue et al.3 and Tanudisastro et al.4 introduce findings from TenK10K’s first phase.

Chelsea are reportedly interested in signing Everton midfielder Harrison Armstrong as Xabi Alonso looks to strengthen his options in the middle of the park ahead of the upcoming transfer windows.

According to Simon Phillips, the Blues have been closely monitoring the 19-year-old and are compiling regular scouting reports on his performances. Chelsea have also contacted his representatives in the past as they assess the possibility of bringing him to Stamford Bridge.

The England Under-21 international has established himself as one of Everton’s most promising young talents, making considerable progress since breaking into the senior squad.

His technical ability, composure in possession and versatility in midfield have attracted attention from several Premier League clubs. Armstrong has already made 32 senior appearances for Everton, providing four assists, and continues to develop into an important player for David Moyes.

Chelsea are looking to invest in young players with considerable potential, and Armstrong could be an exciting long-term addition. Alonso would benefit from having another technically gifted midfielder capable of providing energy and creativity in the centre of the pitch.

The Blues are also monitoring Newcastle United’s Lewis Miley, Fulham’s Josh King and Arsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly as they consider several options in midfield.

Phillips revealed on his YouTube channel: “Chelsea have looked at him in the last couple of windows, and they have actually made contact and spoke to his agents and stuff. So, this is a player that they are definitely very keen on – it’s Myles Lewis-Skelly from Arsenal. So, he is one of the players on this list, but he’s one that we have tracked before.

“The other three are completely new names.”

“Harrison Armstrong of Everton is another youngster that Chelsea are watching. 19 years old, central midfielder, playing quite a bit for Everton this season so far. Got a lot of clubs watching him.”

Phillips added: “The other two names is Josh King from Fulham – central midfielder, England Under-21 international. And then Lewis Miley from Newcastle – another England Under-21 international, plays in midfield, 6ft 2in tall.”

However, convincing Everton to part ways with their academy graduate will not be straightforward. The Toffees previously considered a £40 million offer from Nottingham Forest during the summer, but eventually abandoned the proposed transfer following a strong reaction from supporters.

Armstrong remains under contract at Everton until 2028, putting the Merseyside club in a reasonably strong negotiating position.

The club highly regards the midfielder, and there is little indication they would welcome another approach for his services.

Chelsea are expected to continue monitoring his development through regular scouting reports. Although the youngster fits their recruitment strategy, Everton’s determination to retain him could make negotiations extremely difficult.

#1323. Report Roma have lost Gollini for big Manchester United match

Bad news for Roma, as Pierluigi Gollini has not recovered from a back injury, so they are forced to choose a third-choice goalkeeper against Manchester United in the Champions League.

It kicks off at Old Trafford at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CEST).

There were concerns over the availability of Gollini for tonight’s game after he sustained a back problem during the last training session.

He would be given a late fitness test at the hotel in Manchester, but that proved negative, so Gollini is out of action for this huge fixture.

Gollini was already only filling in for first choice Mile Svilar, who has been out of action for over a month.

Sky Sport Italia, the Corriere dello Sport and more all confirm that the Italian is not available tonight at Old Trafford.

Now coach Gian Piero Gasperini must choose between two options for the third choice goalkeeper to make his season debut tonight.

Former Milan man Devis Vasquez is the favourite, though he was originally not even on the Champions League list, added on after Svilar’s injury.

The Colombian played one competitive match last season, for Besiktas against Karagumruk on April 27.

Another option is 19-year-old Giorgio De Marzi, who plays for the USA at Under-20 level.

There are also growing reports that Leonardo Balerdi and Rodrigo Mora will push into the starting XI for a very attack-minded formation, as Roma aim to make the most of a Manchester United team in crisis.

#1321. How the pandemic changed trust in science — in four charts

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Miryam Naddaf is a reporter for Nature in London.

Science in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: 22% of participants in that nation said they had ‘no trust at all’ in science in 2025. Credit: Thomas Imo/Photothek via Getty

Trust in science and researchers has fallen following the COVID-19 pandemic, the largest survey of public confidence in science shows. Led by the global biomedical funder Wellcome in London and published on 10 October, it explores how people feel about science and health — including vaccines, pandemic preparedness, clean energy and, for the first time, artificial intelligence (see ‘Trust in decline’).

“We should be paying attention to, and thinking about, what needs to be done to earn that trust,” says Philippa Michael, head of public initiatives at Wellcome, who led the project. This is the third survey of its kind conducted by Wellcome, following editions in 2018 and 2020.

The analysis points to a “mixed” picture that varies between countries and regions, says Kathleen Hall Jamieson, a specialist in science communication at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia (see ‘Regional differences’).

The study also shows a connection between science and people’s broader experiences, including their perceived financial security, says Michael (see ’Money matters‘).

“If people feel economically insecure, then they’re going to feel a greater distance between themselves and science and scientists,” says sociologist Gordon Gauchat, at Harvard Kennedy School in Cambridge, Massachusetts. This disconnect “is not about science’s efficacy or its ability to fix problems”, he adds.

The survey found that countries where people reported high confidence in hospitals and health-care clinics were “more likely to have greater trust in science”, notes Michael. Levels of trust were also high in respondents who were confident in accessing health-care services when needed. “It’s really essential that science is credible, relevant and beneficial to people in their lives,” Michael adds.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03248-z

#1320. Official: Malagò vs. Galliani for FIGC President election on Dec 14

Giovanni Malagò has filed his candidacy for the fresh December 14 election as FIGC President and will be against former Milan and Monza chief Adriano Galliani.

Malagò of course had already won a landslide election in June, but that was declared null and void on October 6 because he did not have the right paperwork to run for the FIGC role.

He was instead given a new role as the FIGC special commissioner that same day, a way of providing continuity and in theory this was meant to tide him over until another election could be held, this time with the proper registration.

However, since then several parties who had backed his candidacy the first time have changed their minds, and are now supporting Galliani for the Presidency.

They include the Players’ Association and the Coaches’ Association, who have formally backed Galliani.

Today, Malagò formally filed his candidacy, co-signed by 11 Serie A clubs.

November 4 is the deadline for candidates, after which we can go into the new election on December 14.

#1318. Champions League line-ups: Feyenoord vs. Inter

Inter badly need to revive their Champions League fortunes with a difficult trip to Feyenoord, as Francesco Pio Esposito, Federico Dimarco and Djed Spence start.

It kicks off at the Stadion De Kuip in Rotterdam at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from this game and Manchester United vs. Roma on the Liveblog.

The mood in the Nerazzurri camp is dismal after losing the Derby della Madonnina 3-1 to Milan at the weekend, their first Serie A defeat of the season which knocked them three points off leaders Lazio.

Their Champions League form had already been raising eyebrows, losing the first two fixtures to Real Madrid and Club Brugge, then scraping a 1-0 victory over Shakhtar Donetsk when down to 10 men.

Alessandro Bastoni was sent off in that game and is therefore suspended here, with Lautaro Martinez, Curtis Jones, Luis Henrique and John Stones still injured.

Choices were very limited in the derby because of a flu bug sweeping through the squad, but Pio Esposito has recovered and is able to start with Marcus Thuram.

Dimarco and Piotr Zielinski also return to the starting XI, while Benjamin Pavard is at least an option off the bench now.

Spence keeps the right wing-back role, with Hakan Calhanoglu and Nicolò Barella in midfield.

Feyenoord have already beaten Como here in the Champions League, confirming they are a very different side on home turf.

They have quite a few injuries to deal with this evening, missing Jakub Moder, Bart Nieuwkoop, Gijs Smal, Jeremiah St. Juste, Thomas Beelen and Jordan Bos.

Anis Hadj Moussa was very impressive in the game against Como, and is certainly one to watch attacking Dimarco down that flank.

These teams faced off in the Champions League Round of 16 last season, Inter winning 2-0 away and 2-1 at San Siro.

Kevin Ochsner is at the Center for Brain, Mind and Society, Columbia University, New York City, New York 10027, USA.

The ability to manage difficult feelings is so essential to everyday life that failures to regulate emotion effectively are associated with detrimental social, occupational and physical-health outcomes. One of the most well-studied regulation strategies is cognitive reappraisal, in which a person changes how they think about an event to alter its emotional impact — for example, finding the ‘silver lining’. Writing in Nature, Sicorello et al.1 investigate an assumption that researchers have held about measuring reappraisal.

Roma are forced to pick third choice goalkeeper Devis Vasquez, but Donyell Malen, Rodrigo Mora and Matias Soulé face Manchester United and Bruno Fernandes in the Champions League.

It kicks off at Old Trafford at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CEST).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from this game and Feyenoord vs. Inter on the Liveblog.

The Giallorossi lost only one competitive match all season, the 4-3 defeat to Real Madrid when they had been leading 3-1 going into the 82nd minute.

They are still missing Paulo Dybala, Mile Svilar, Manu Koné and Lorenzo Pellegrini, but the hours leading up to this game were dominated by concern over second choice goalkeeper Gollini.

He was struggling with a back injury sustained during the final training session, and failed a fitness test, with the only other options Devis Vasquez and 19-year-old Giorgio De Marzi.

Elsewhere, Rodrigo Mora and Soulé support hitman Malen for a very attack-minded team.

Devyne Rensch and Wesley take up the wings, with Leonardo Balerdi stepping into the back three rather than Evan N’Dicka.

Manchester United are in pure crisis with many assuming this might be the last chance for Michael Carrick to save his job.

It would be an opportunity for revenge, as Carrick scored twice when Manchester United beat Roma 7-1 in 2007.

They sit 17th in the Premier League with just seven points from nine rounds and are without a victory since the 4-0 Champions League result with Sabah FK on September 10.

That was followed by three draws and six defeats in all competition, including a 4-1 hammering by Como.

They’ve lost their last three games on the bounce, scoring one goal and conceding nine.

Lenny Yoro is available again after his suspension against Como, but Benjamin Sesko, Patrick Dorgu, Marcus Rashford, Manuel Ugarte and Luke Shaw are still out of action.

Bruno Fernandes was benched against Bournemouth as a result of his post-Como criticism of Carrick’s tactics, but returned to the starting XI for the 2-0 defeat to Chelsea at the weekend.

Manchester United: Lammens; Yoro, Maguire, Heaven, Dalot; Mainoo, Baleba; Amad Diallo, Bruno Fernandes, Cunha; Mbeumo

Manchester United bench: Darlow, Heaton, Mazraoui, De Ligt, Lisandro Martinez, Mount, Zirkzee, Andrey Santos, Tielemans, Lacey, T Fletcher, Amass

Roma: Vasquez; Mancini, Balerdi, Hermoso; Rensch, Cristante, De Roon, Wesley; Soulé, Mora; Malen

Roma bench: De Marzi, Koulierakis, N’Dicka, Castro, Molina, Pisilli, Di Nunzio, Lulli, Ghilardi

#1314. RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: Here's what I've heard privately about Max Dowman that proves he will come out of Mikel Arteta scolding a stronger player - and why he'll have dealt with far worse already

Published: 22:00 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 06:47 EDT, 2 November 2026

Mikel Arteta didn’t require the hysteria of the past week to know a thing or two about dubious reactions. Before we get onto his reaction to Max Dowman’s reaction, or the wider reaction to those reactions, we might revisit something that happened in November 2010.

That’s a long journey into the past, but the episode tells us a little about Arteta’s feelings for opponents who took liberties with his shins. The abbreviated version: violence would be returned with spectacular amounts of interest.

The longer telling revolves around a match between Arteta’s Everton and West Brom. To rewatch some of the footage now, we would say Gonzalo Jara brought it upon himself after 58 minutes, when in a mad passage he elbowed Leighton Baines and then barged shoulder-first into Steven Pienaar in the same scramble for a loose ball.

The defining act came next – Arteta stepped in to retrieve possession, but was clattered by Jara with one of those nasty scissor-motion tackles that could break the standing leg. If that sounds familiar, it’s because the challenge was near-identical to the lunge by Fleetwood Town’s Harrison Neal that provoked Dowman on Tuesday night.

But Arteta didn’t kick Jara, as Dowman did Neal. No, he stomped on his leg. Twice, actually. And with venom in each.

Arsenal's 16-year-old Max Dowman gets an earful from his manager Mikel Arteta after the attacker was sent off on Tuesday night against Fleetwood

It was a frustrating night for Dowman who failed to live up to the excitement that surrounds him

Dowman was around 11 months old when this happened, so he’ll have no idea about all that. And besides, he’d probably be wise to avoid bringing it up. Aged 16, his sense of which battles to pick will be growing by the hour.

But Arteta was 28 when he turned vigilante against West Brom. And it wasn’t quite an isolated incident.

Seven months earlier, Morten Gamst Pedersen stepped on Arteta’s ankle in a game against Blackburn and the Spaniard didn’t like it. His response? He poked Pedersen in the eye and got a yellow.

So let’s offer a couple of conclusions at this point.

One is about Arteta – if he wishes to present himself as a poster boy for the zen state and self-control in football matches, then he might need to torch a few archives. The two yellow cards he has collected on the touchline this season would suggest his own journey to enlightenment is ongoing.

The second, more meaningful conclusion centres on the general theme that Dowman should have been preserved from a few chilly words and a colder stare from his manager.

In the aftermath of Arsenal’s defeat at Fleetwood, that peculiar stance has been propagated by Paul Merson and Gabby Agbonlahor, who were among the vocal cohort that bristled and recoiled at the sight of a young pro being sent to the dressing room without a cuddle. The backlash against Arteta almost sounded as if he had abdicated a duty of care. Of all the reactions in this saga, I found that the strangest.

When Arteta addressed the matter on Friday, his justification felt far closer to the mark: ‘You have to understand the context. We’re not in Disneyland, we’re in the Premier League.'

If Arteta wishes to present himself as a poster boy for the zen state and self-control in football matches, then he might wish to explain why he gets booked so often

Morten Gamst Pedersen is left reeling after a clash with Arteta in his Everton days. A few years later Arteta would poke Pedersen in the eye during a game at Ewood Park

A hypocrite on the subject of retaliations? Yes, we can go with that. Wrong in his handling of a young player who lost his cool? No. Definitely not.

At 16, we can say Dowman meets the legal definition of a child, and a bloody talented one at that, but he’s not a kid. Kids don’t get into the Arsenal first team. Kids wouldn’t survive the hothouse of a Premier League academy.

To understand why that might be, it is instructive to look back to an update on the Arsenal website from the summer. On June 4, as they do every year, they put out a few words to detail which of their Under 18s and Under 21s had not made the grade, which was a list that included the names of Harrison Dudziak, Seb Ferdinand, Cam’ron Ismail, Will Sweet and Josh Nichols.

As very good players, they were all in the Arsenal Under 19s squad in 2024, when Dowman, aged 14, became the youngest scorer in the UEFA Youth League's history against Atalanta.

Of the starting XI that day, only four remain at Arsenal, and the point is this – Dowman has lived through the brutalities of that whittling process every summer and he will have been friends with those who had their dreams ended.

He will have been hardened by their traumas and solidified by knowing what it takes to stay standing in that world.

In short, when we attempt to imagine his position, and wonder how a cold shoulder might feel to a Gen Z child in the Arsenal team, we do so without the relevant context.

Because Dowman was never in Disneyland. A Premier League academy, even an excellent and caring one like that at Arsenal, will inevitably be more like a trip to the Hunger Games. Dowman has been there since he was five, so let’s assume it will take more than a mildly disappointed manager to hurt his feelings.

An incensed Dowman grapples with the Fleetwood Town players just before being sent off on Tuesday night

Dowman has not appeared flustered while he has passed milestones at breakneck speed in his short career so far

Based on everything I’ve heard privately and publicly about Dowman, his reaction to the reaction chain will go the other way. He’s a tremendously promising player and has a strong mind with good people behind him – it’s why he has not been flustered by any of the milestones he has passed at breakneck speed.

The wobbles, like the one at Fleetwood and shortly before that with England Under 19s, are few. But they are also useful, based on the truism that we all learn more when things go wrong. Viewed through that lens, Arteta’s worst possible response would be to indulge a blip or pretend it never happened. As an excellent manager, he hasn’t done that.

It is too early to say how far Dowman will go in his career. Likewise, we have no idea if he will shape into the kind of player who jabs a finger into the occasional eye or plants studs in any thighs. His reaction to Neal on Tuesday was certainly at the Disney-end of that scale.

But Dowman’s chances of succeeding will only be increased by learning where the margins exist. As with a few other facets of his game, he is ahead of the curve.

A confession: I find the Kylian Mbappe ‘dictator’ memes funny. If you haven’t seen them, the gist is pretty simple – someone once decided that he carries himself like a dictator and subsequently imposed his head on the bodies and uniforms of a few notorious figures from history.

One of those was Chairman Mao Zedong and Mbappe’s own amusement at that fact is why he was forced onto the journey of 1,000 apologies this week.

In China, where it remains taboo to query Mao’s actions in any way, Mbappe has since had multiple sponsorships cancelled and a diplomatic row has swirled, with the upshot that a state-controlled broadcaster is now refusing to screen his matches.

The space here is too short to relitigate the deaths of millions of people under Mao’s reign, but Mbappe might have cause to wonder if he ever really needed Chinese money that badly.

Kylian Mbappe got himself into hot water this week by finding a Chairman Mao meme amusing. He has now had sponsorship deals in China canned

With a tail tucked between his legs, Sergio Garcia has announced his return to the DP World Tour after the demise of LIV.

Aside from saying he is ‘proud’ to be going back, Garcia adds that he is ‘excited’ to ‘strengthen personal relationships’ with those he left behind in 2022.

Based on multiple conversations I have had with leading players from the Tour, including a well-known name who has regularly described Garcia as a ‘total a**e’ since his defection, that excitement is remarkably one-sided.

#1313. 15 Most Skilful English Players in Football History [Ranked]

England may not be the first country that springs to mind when you think of skillful footballers, but among the tough tacklers and target men up top, you will find some of the silkiest players to have played the beautiful game.

The English game has seen some wonderfully adept tricksters down the years, capturing the hearts and minds of those that follow the Three Lions. From the wizardry of the likes of Glenn Hoddle to the skill and talent of Paul Gascoigne, England's brightest stars are often the most skilful. With that in mind, here are the 15 most skillful players to pull on the famous England jersey.

From Steven Gerrard to Paul Scholes, here are the best passers from England in football history.

Whilst a transfer to Manchester United may not have spelled out great fortune for Jadon Sancho, there is little denying that he is one of the more well-known players for tricks and flair to have come from England. The South-London born winger made his name at the Watford and Manchester City academies, before being picked up in 2017 by Bundesliga giants Borussia Dortmund.

Sancho turned out over 100 times for the German side, and quickly outed himself as one of the trickiest, most eye-catching wingers in the world. Loan spells at Chelsea and Aston Villa later brought Conference League and Europa League winners' medals, and his appearance in Villa's 2026 final made him the first player to feature in three consecutive European finals for three different clubs in three different competitions.

Though his performances for Manchester United and bad luck in the Premier League hold him down in this list, he is more than deserving of a spot on it regardless, due to his initial rise.

Jadon Sancho's farewell messages to Man United and Borussia Dortmund couldn't be more different after the 24-year-old made his Chelsea switch.

Small, deceptive and endlessly inventive, Peter Beardsley is regarded as England's first recognised number 10. Turned away after trials at Gillingham, Burnley and Cambridge United, he became the subject of a British record £1.9 million fee when Kenny Dalglish brought him to Liverpool in 1987, forming a devastating front line alongside John Barnes and John Aldridge that won two league titles and the FA Cup.

His close control and feints made him a favourite wherever he went, from two spells at Newcastle, the second as one of Kevin Keegan's Entertainers, to Everton, where he became one of only two players to score for both sides in the Merseyside derby. For England, he won 59 caps and proved Gary Lineker's ideal foil across two World Cups.

Though known today for his questionable punditry takes, Michael Owen's ridiculous ability at the peak of his powers should never be forgotten.

Known for his clinical goalscoring and intense pace, Owen's small stature and quick feet had him outed as one of the most technically gifted and trickiest forwards in English history, with his exploits seeing him join up with Los Blancos in 2004 for a year. It's little surprise, then, that the Chester-born forward received the coveted Ballon d'Or in 2001; the last Englishman to win the award to date.

Carragher probably won't thank Owen for revealing this

One of the most stylish and world-known footballers to have ever graced the sport, David Beckham was one of the most technically gifted footballers to have partaken in the sport.

Whilst many know him for his world-famous set-piece and crossing abilities, brandished by the term "Bend it like Beckham", his ability with the ball at his feet is something that should not slip down in terms of how it is recognised. As a counter-point to his explosive Manchester United winger partner Ryan Giggs, Beckham's strength lay in his passing and movement to beat his opponents, with a wide-range of sharp skills that allowed him to perform to his creative best.

The Spanish top flight has been home to some of the best players England have ever produced.

Few English players have made the difficult look as effortless as Cole Palmer. Nicknamed 'Cold Palmer' for his composure, the Wythenshawe-born playmaker came through Manchester City's academy and was part of their 2022/23 treble-winning squad before a £40 million move to Chelsea unlocked his talent.

His debut season at Stamford Bridge brought 22 Premier League goals, 11 assists and the PFA Young Player of the Year award, and he followed it by becoming the first player in Premier League history to score four times in a single first half, against Brighton in 2024. Palmer saves his best for the biggest occasions, too: he struck England's equaliser from outside the box in the Euro 2024 final, then scored twice and assisted once as Chelsea beat PSG 3-0 in the 2025 Club World Cup final, collecting the tournament's Golden Ball.

Arsène Wenger once described Jack Wilshere as a player blessed with Spanish technique and an English heart, and at his peak few English midfielders could glide through a crowded centre circle quite like him. Arsenal's youngest-ever league debutant at 16 years and 256 days, he won the PFA Young Player of the Year award for 2010/11.

His signature moment came against Norwich in 2013, a slick sequence of one-touch passing finished off by Wilshere himself, which was voted Goal of the Season. He won the award again the following year, the first player to do so in back-to-back seasons in the Premier League era. Injuries ultimately robbed him of a career at the very top, but 34 England caps and two FA Cups hint at what might have been.

One of the earliest 'Galactico' signings, Steve McManaman was a fiercely talented operator. A two-time Champions League winner with Real Madrid, McManaman's dazzling footwork and deep box of tricks carved him out as one of the finer wingers in Europe, with the ability to glide past defenders with ease, coupled with a keen eye for a pass.

After a glittering 566-appearance career for three top clubs, McManaman brought the curtain down on his playing days in 2005.

Remembered first for the goals, Sir Bobby Charlton was also among the most gifted ball-carriers England has ever produced. Starting out as a quick, agile outside-left, he grew into an attacking midfielder capable of running long distances with the ball under control before unleashing a ferocious shot with either foot.

A survivor of the 1958 Munich air disaster, Charlton went on to make 758 appearances and score 249 goals for Manchester United, captaining them to European Cup glory in 1968 with two goals in the final against Benfica. Two years earlier, he had been central to England's World Cup triumph and won the Ballon d'Or. His 106 caps and 49 goals stood as national records for years, and remarkably, he was booked only twice in his entire career.

The first ever winner of the Ballon d'Or, Stanley Matthews possessed an air of grace, poise and skill that far belied the generation in which he played in.

Franz Beckenbauer once stated that Matthews possessed such speed and skill that "almost no-one in the game could stop him". Johnny Giles claimed that he had everything – "good close control, great dribbling ability. He was lightning quick. He was also an intelligent player, who knew how to pass the ball". Those who witnessed him and his revolutionary training methods and style of play all remarked Matthews as one of the silkiest of all time. A hero of yesteryear, whose mark on the English game stands forever more.

Cristiano Ronaldo does not make the list of the 15 most technically gifted players in football history.

Nicknamed 'Magic Chris', the former Spurs and Marseille talisman was widely regarded as one of the finest, silkiest attacking midfielders in all of Europe.

With 62 caps for England, and at one point being made the third-most expensive player in the world following his French switch from Tottenham, Waddle was gifted from the off with his outstanding skillset and creative abilities. Born through a deep-bred love for the game, Waddle took to every game with a unique flair and air of confidence, even when he turned out for non-league Hallam FC in his fifties.

England has been home to several unique entertainers who weren't afraid to push the boundaries with their elite dribbling skills.

#1312. Fabregas: ‘Como will face wild atmosphere in Lens, quality of Thauvin’

Cesc Fabregas warns Como that there will be a ‘wild atmosphere’ against RC Lens in the Champions League tomorrow and he is keeping a close eye on Florian Thauvin.

It kicks off at the Stade Bollaert-Delelis in Lens on Wednesday at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CET).

The Lariani are in their first ever Champions League campaign and doing remarkably well, winning both home matches with four goals scored against RB Leipzig and Manchester United, but losing away to Feyenoord.

While RC Lens might not seem to be on paper as big as those sides, Fabregas warns they are not to be underestimated on home turf.

“It’s a wild atmosphere, I played here two or three times for Monaco, I love nights like this, because you can feel the passion even during the warm-up,” Fabregas told Sky Sport Italia.

“It will be interesting and a marvellous experience for our players. We wanted these nights, so if you are not motivated to play these, then you’re in the wrong job.”

There is a familiar face to Italian football, as former Udinese man Florian Thauvin has flourished since his return to France.

“Thauvin is an incredible player, he was at Marseille, then we faced him for Udinese. He makes the difference, has huge quality, scores a lot of goals, so he is the reference point for this team, and we need to keep a close eye on him.”

Como are perhaps no longer a surprise outfit at this stage, so what will their ambitions be if they win here tomorrow?

“We will try to win and then see what happens, but this season is a whole new experience for Como, our world is opening up. If we get a good result, then we’ll see how to go into the final four games, but we have to keep taking it one game at a time,” added Fabregas.

“There’s no point thinking about what might happen, we just need to enjoy these nights.”

While Como would in the past need to score lots of goals to win fixtures, they seem to have found different ways of approaching tests now.

“We need to be able to handle different situations. We played 39 games the first season, 43 the second, this year it’ll be at least 47-48, it might be over 50, so that means we need to balance out the energy.

“There are moments where we need to control the situation, because I remember last season we were great for the first 60 minutes and then fell away at the end. We cannot do that this term, so we’re more alert about that.”

Como also have a huge game coming up in Serie A against Inter this weekend, but they have limited players available, with Trevoh Chalobah, Moise Kean, Jesus Rodriguez, Assane Diao and Jayden Addai out of action.

“Chalobah isn’t ready for this game, we’ll see on Sunday. We are a little penalised in the Champions League because of the list, so we’ve got only 15 players tomorrow. That makes preserving energy tougher in this tournament, but Serie A remains the most important competition.”

Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel died as a result of a freak accident during the Spanish second division match against FC Andorra, so Fabregas wanted to send a message.

“In such a wonderful sport as football, it is honestly hard to deal with things like this. I send my heart to his father and mother, I am a parent, and the idea of going to see your son playing in a match and life can end in a moment, it makes you think.

“It was a huge blow, I cannot imagine the pain they are feeling, so I send an embrace to his family, to his teammates who experienced that, it can never be forgotten.”

#1310. Every British Ballon d’Or Winner [Ranked]

The Ballon d'Or is the single biggest individual award there is to win in European football. Ever since its introduction in 1956, the Golden Ball has been the standard-bearer for every great player who has and does make a living on the continent.

Winning it isn't something many can claim, which is exactly why so few names from the British Isles appear on the roll of honour. Seven men from England, Scotland and Northern Ireland have, at some stage of their careers, held the title of the best player on the planet. Despite the best efforts of Ryan Giggs and Gareth Bale, Wales, unfortunately, is still waiting.

Ranking the greatest of that select group meant weighing up a number of different factors rather than picking a favourite.

Because these six played in such different eras, the following was taken into account when building the list:

While an incredible player at his peak, it is hard to argue that Michael Owen was a surprising recipient of this award. The four years prior had seen Ronaldo, Zinedine Zidane, Rivaldo and Luis Figo win the Ballon d'Or. The season that Owen won the award, Liverpool weren't even in the Champions League.

By today's standards, that gap alone would likely end his chances before voting even began, since a player with no real Champions League impact rarely gets serious consideration now. Even so, Owen deserves real credit: he saw off the likes of Raul and Oliver Kahn, both major names in their own right, to land the prize.

Long before Eric Cantona earned the nickname 'King of Old Trafford', Denis Law held that status. The Scot formed one third of Manchester United's famous Holy Trinity, alongside two players who feature elsewhere on this list.

Law was all about one thing. Goals. United signed him from Torino to add a ruthless streak up top and he most certainly did. The year he won the Ballon d'Or, he pipped some serious other candidates, including Jimmy Greaves and Eusebio, both of whom missed out on the top 3. Today, his legacy stands as one of Scotland's greatest-ever players.

He's the man who started it all. Stoke City and Blackpool great Sir Stanley Matthews was the very first player ever handed the Ballon d'Or. Born just a little later, he'd surely have had a role to play in England's 1966 World Cup triumph.

GIVEMESPORT Key Statistic: Stanley Matthews is the oldest ever Ballon d'Or winner at 41.

As it was, Matthews was already into his 50s by the time Sir Alf Ramsey guided the Three Lions to glory, having hung up his boots only a year earlier. Being the award's inaugural winner is enough to see him placed just ahead of Owen and Law here.

The biggest individual prize in football is won by players at differing stages of their career, young and old - here's the best older winners ranked.

Having toiled for years with trophyless Tottenham, Harry Kane took his game to a whole new level when he moved to Bayern Munich in 2023 and England's all-time leading goalscorer got the recognition he deserved in 2026 as he won the Ballon d'Or ahead of the likes of Kylian Mbappe, Lamine Yamal and Lionel Messi. Kane scored 73 goals for club and country during the voting period, winning the European Golden Shoe in 2025/26 and helping Bayern to a Bundesliga and DFB Pokal double.

20 different countries have produced at least one winner of the prestigious honour, but which nation has produced the most?

Britain's only ever two-time Ballon d'Or winner, and in consecutive years too. That is some going for Newcastle hero Kevin Keegan. The forward was a European Cup and First Division champion at Liverpool not long before he got ahold of the Golden Ball, but he was actually plying his trade in Germany when he was crowned the best player in the world.

He'd joined Hamburg back in 1977, and it was his second triumph there that carried more weight. Keegan cruised to victory over Bayern Munich's Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, who would then claim the award himself in each of the following two years.

"Pele called me the greatest footballer in the world. That is the ultimate salute to my life." Those were George Best's words and perhaps one of the biggest compliments the Northern Irish hero could have been paid. Best's demons off the pitch are well-known and a sad story. But on the pitch, he was nothing but a fairytale.

Some of the all-time great entertainers have come from the British isles. Here are the best 11.

Fear simply wasn't part of his game, and more often than not defenders were left with no answer for him. It didn't matter if six players stood between him and goal — his dribbling was good enough to leave them all for dead. The year he lifted the trophy, United's 'Busby Babes' had just won the club's first European Cup, a run in which Best played a vital part throughout.

Is he England's greatest-ever player? Is he Manchester United's? Both are debates that will run forever, but whichever way they land, Bobby Charlton's name belongs in the conversation. A midfielder who scored like a natural-born striker, he once held the all-time scoring record for both his club and his country simultaneously.

He was also, alongside Bobby Moore, the most pivotal piece of the puzzle when England bought home the World Cup at Wembley Stadium, with his impact such that the legendary Franz Beckenbauer was given the job to man-mark his opposite number. Aside from his 1966 win, the European Cup winner also finished runner-up the following two years by the smallest of margins. As such, Charlton's place at number one is well and truly cemented.

#1309. Chivu: ‘Inter need intensity, determination and grit’ against Feyenoord

Cristian Chivu warns Inter that Feyenoord ‘are a different team’ at home and his side ‘cannot afford to play without determination and grit’ in the Champions League.

It kicks off at the Stadion De Kuip in Rotterdam at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from this game and Manchester United vs. Roma on the Liveblog.

The mood in the Nerazzurri camp is one of concern after a series of poor performances, culminating in the 3-1 Derby della Madonnina defeat to Milan on Saturday evening.

They were already under pressure in the Champions League after losing the first two matches to Real Madrid and Club Brugge, then scraped a 1-0 win over Shakhtar Donetsk when down to 10 men.

Alessandro Bastoni was sent off in that game and is therefore suspended this evening, with Lautaro Martinez, Curtis Jones, Luis Henrique and John Stones still injured.

“It is a tough environment, the fans give a lot and we know they are a different team at home with intensity, so we must be ready to face adversity and situations we cannot afford to handle without determination and grit,” Chivu told Sky Sport Italia.

“We need quality, intensity both defending and attacking, the wing-backs who need to time the runs properly, passes to the strikers. We can’t know what will happen, but we are prepared for any situation.”

Djed Spence didn’t play for months after representing England at the World Cup, but now he is regularly in the starting XI for Inter, so is this an attempt to get him back to full fitness?

“Spence is ready to play another 90 minutes of quality,” assured Chivu.

There is a huge Serie A match coming up this weekend against Como, which is starting to become almost a Scudetto showdown.

#1308. Golden Boy 2026: Date, Nominees & Where to Watch

The race to crown the sport's next prodigy is nearing its end, as European football prepares to name the 2026 Golden Boy. The most coveted accolade for any of the best young players in world football, the award has often provided a precursor to widespread success in professional football.

Anticipation and debate over who could secure the award has been amplified with the reveal of the 25-man shortlist. After an incredible World Cup, another Champions League triumph for Paris Saint-Germain, and a highly competitive Premier League campaign, the nominees are reflective of the depth of talent currently found in Europe's elite leagues.

Ahead of the gala, here are all the key details for those hoping to tune into the event.

The Golden Boy ceremony, one of the key dates in the 2026/27 football season, will take place on December 14 2026, in Turin, Italy. The winner of the award will be announced prior to the ceremony, with the reveal expected to take place mid-November.

Fans can tune into official streams on the Tuttosport website and the publication's YouTube channel, while major European sports networks are also expected to broadcast the gala live.

The most gifted young footballers on the planet have been ranked in order.

Whilst the likes of Barcelona, Real Madrid, and Chelsea have multiple entries on the list, there are a few surprise inclusions from less prominent teams. Bournemouth and Brighton will be celebrating two nominees each after impressive Premier League campaigns. The Bundesliga is also well represented with five nominees — only one of whom plays for champions Bayern Munich.

Previous winners Desire Doue and Lamine Yamal have performed well enough to be nominated, but due to the award's strict ruling that a player can only win the Golden Boy once, they have not been shortlisted.

The Premier League is well represented with eight nominees on the shortlist — more than any other league in Europe. However, despite winning the Premier League and reaching the Champions League final (as well as having several eligible players), Arsenal have just one nominee on the list.

Who will be taking Desire Doue's crown in 2026?

Established in 2003 by the Italian newspaper Tuttosport, the Golden Boy was created to recognize the most outstanding under-21 footballer playing in a top-tier European league over a calendar year. With that in mind, the judging period considers performances from the second half of the previous season (2025/26) and the opening months of the current season (2026/27).

The winner is decided by a panel of 50 sports journalists representing leading newspapers and media outlets across Europe. These include L'Équipe, Marca, Bild, The Times, and De Telegraaf. Each journalist votes for five players, distributing points (10, 7, 5, 3, and 1) to determine the overall winner. Additionally, football fans can vote separately online to determine the winner of the Golden Boy Web Award.

The 25-man shortlist that the journalists choose from is determined using the Golden Boy Index, which is developed by Football Benchmark. The criteria included in the index takes into account the quality of the team they play for, the minutes completed by the player, and their performance level. The index ranking also considers how well the players fare in European and international tournaments, such as the Champions League and the World Cup.

The honour roll for past Golden Boy winners is a who's who of the very best talents in European football over the past two decades. Dutch midfielder Rafael van der Vaart was the inaugural winner in 2003, and the likes of Lionel Messi, Sergio Aguero, and Wayne Rooney received the award before going on to have incredible careers.

Over the last decade, many of the current crop of top-tier stars won the award at the beginning of their promising careers. Kylian Mbappe, Erling Haaland, and Jude Bellingham are also past recipients of the award.

👑 GOLDEN BOY: Who should win the 2026 award?

The winners of the Golden Boy award have experienced mixed career paths.

#1307. Roma ‘have faith in Vasquez’ against Manchester United amid new problems

Roma director Tony D’Amico assures they ‘have faith’ in third choice goalkeeper Devis Vasquez against Manchester United and reveals why Gian Piero Gasperini didn’t speak to the media.

It kicks off at Old Trafford at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CEST).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from this game and Feyenoord vs. Inter on the Liveblog.

The Giallorossi were shaken by fresh injury problems just hours before the match, as goalkeeper Pierluigi Gollini hurt his back in the last training session.

He was given pain-killing injections, but they were not sufficient, so Devis Vasquez had to step in as their third choice, seeing as Mile Svilar has already been out of action for a month.

It was originally meant to be coach Gasperini who held the media duties pre-match, but seeing as Roma were late getting to the stadium due to traffic in Manchester, it was decided that director of sport D’Amico would take over.

“We took longer than expected to get here without a police escort, but we’re here now, these things happen,” D’Amico told Sky Sport Italia.

“Gollini felt back pain this morning, we tried to get him back in shape, but didn’t manage it, we have faith in Vasquez. This is an opportunity for him, he is one of the four goalkeepers at our disposal and these things happen.

“He will have a big chance and we are confident he can have a good game.”

This is only the latest setback for a side that is already missing Paulo Dybala, Manu Koné and Lorenzo Pellegrini too.

Nonetheless, they have lost only one match all season, the 4-3 defeat to Real Madrid in a game they were leading 3-1 going into the 82nd minute.

#1306. How Many Games Jesus Owono Could Be Banned For After Colliding with Jesus de Miguel

How many games Jesus Owono could be set to miss after colliding with Jesus de Miguel has now emerged, following the striker's tragic passing early on Tuesday morning.

CD Tenerife had initially provided a worrying update on their player's neurological condition at 4am local time, confirming that De Miguel had suffered a cardiac arrest after taking a high knee from the opposition goalkeeper.

Four hours later, it was announced that he had passed away in hospital, having been rushed there after his side's Spanish second-tier clash against FC Andorra, which was poised at 2-2, had been abandoned following the distressing scenes.

An update has since emerged on Owono, with the goalkeeper reportedly seen 'crying and praying' in the dressing room after the shocking incident. And now, with Spanish police having launched an investigation, the potential punishment he could face has been outlined.

According to Guillem Balague, a renowned Spanish journalist, the RFEF has suspended today's Cup matchday, some of which had already been moved a week because of the Urda train accident.

Tenerife have asked to postpone Saturday's League game against Granada and Tuesday's Cup tie against Badajoz, and the League and RFEF are expected to accept that request. Ballague also wrote (See his full post below):

"[Jesus] Owono faces a ban of four to eight matches, or even more for the extreme consequence of his clash with de Miguel."

.Any current footballing investigations will likely look towards the intent of the 25-year-old Equatorial Guinea international, though any legal action is currently considered unlikely.

As per the same report, it is unlikely that Owono will face criminal charges that many on social media - mainly through online abuse directed at the goalkeeper - have called for.

Police have launched an investigation because there has been a death, and that always happens as standard protocol, but it is almost impossible that anything comes of it.

As per Ballague, the tackle was a circumstance of the game, and Spanish Supreme Court doctrine (STS 379/2025) only brings in criminal law where there was clear intent to hurt, and it isn't related to the game.

#1305. Could a giant sunshade in space ‘solve global warming’? Scientists are taking the idea seriously

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Researchers say that a ‘planetary sunshade’ placed between Earth and the Sun could cool down the planet by 1 °C.Credit: Mongpro/Getty

In August, entrepreneur Elon Musk suggested in a social-media post that Earth could be cooled by launching satellites into space to shade the planet from the Sun. These “sentient satellites”, he wrote, “can solve global warming for ~1B years”.

Climate engineering faces hostility — here’s how scientists say it might move forwards

Climate engineering faces hostility — here’s how scientists say it might move forwards

It’s unclear whether Musk, chief executive of the aerospace firm SpaceX in Starbase, Texas, meant for this to be taken seriously. But some researchers are earnestly investigating space-based methods of reflecting sunlight away from Earth to cool the planet as temperatures rise to increasingly dangerous levels.

A non-profit organization called the Planetary Sunshade Institute in Los Angeles, California, published a report this month that researchers say is the most detailed analysis yet of such geoengineering methods. The report — which summarizes studies from a consortium of engineers and climate scientists, including some from leading space agencies such as NASA — estimates that it could become viable to begin building a ‘planetary sunshade’ in as few as 20–40 years. The timeline would depend on the rate at which heavy-lift rockets are developed that can haul millions of tonnes of material into deep space to create the sunshade. (SpaceX, which is not involved in the report, did not respond to a query from Nature about whether it is conducting research on this topic.)

A lot of people think this idea is “just fantasy”, says Chantal Cappelletti, a space-systems engineer at the University of Nottingham, UK, who is part of the consortium. But the falling cost of space launches have made the prospect seem more feasible, she says.

Blocking sunlight to cool the planet through solar geoengineering has long been controversial. Proposals have included releasing sunlight-reflecting particles into Earth’s atmosphere, which could affect the planet in poorly understood ways, such as disrupting precipitation and plant growth. Space-based approaches could come with unique risks, including the pollution unleashed from many thousands of rocket launches. Critics also say that focusing attention on geoengineering distracts from the urgent need to cut greenhouse-gas emissions to address climate change.

Controversial geoengineering projects to test Earth-cooling tech funded by UK agency

Controversial geoengineering projects to test Earth-cooling tech funded by UK agency

But solar geoengineering has received more attention from researchers as Earth looks set to hurtle past 1.5 °C of warming above the planet’s pre-industrial baseline temperature. The “accelerating climate crisis” is pushing the world towards solar geoengineering, says Morgan Goodwin, a climate activist and executive director of the Planetary Sunshade Institute.

The report is the group’s biggest project so far, funded by a £400,000 (US$530,000) grant from the UK Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA), a body sponsored by the government to fund high-risk, high-reward research. That grant is part of a larger £56.8-million ARIA research programme on solar geoengineering.

Daniele Visioni, a climate scientist at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, says that he had previously dismissed space-based approaches as science fiction. But after attending an engineering workshop on such approaches earlier this year, he was persuaded that they deserve more attention. However, “I still wouldn’t put this as something feasible before the end of the century”, he says.
